speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity, short as it is, to say a few words today on the motion presented by my colleague from Essex-Windsor. His motion was essentially on the state of the economy on the eve of the budget, which will be presented by the Minister of Finance on Monday afternoon.
I would like to take this opportunity to say a few words about the general state of affairs of the economy in the country. I would also like to draw some conclusions and comment about the general national state and mention a
Supply
few situations that I think bear some relevance in my riding to the debate we are having today.
There is no question that the time is quickly coming for this government and all Canadians to take a strong look at the choices that are available to address the problems facing our economy. It is important to get the message across that there are choices. They may not be the choices this government has made nor the choices of other critics of this government, but there are real choices and real positive solutions to some of the problems we face in this country today.
I do not think anyone, particularly on the government side, should reject or hide from the fact that we are in a very difficult economic situation. Unemployment in March rose to 11 per cent from 10.8 per cent in the previous month.
Amazingly there are some 1.5 million people in Canada looking for work. Our unemployment rate last year was the highest of all the G-7 countries. My leader, the member for Yukon, has mentioned in her questions to the finance minister that in addition to the unemployed we have the problem of the underemployed. That is often not addressed or dealt with in this House and I think it is important that it be raised, as does the leader of the New Democratic Party.
We have also seen the explosion of the welfare rolls all across the country. The point made by our leader in the House has been in response to the government challenging the opposition to offer alternatives. When we have been presented with that challenge we have offered alternatives.
Alternatives were presented by our party in the extensive debate we had on the goods and services tax in this House. We were the only party to do that. We met that challenge and I suggest that we bested the government in terms of what we said could be done.
With regard to the welfare rolls, a question has been put to the finance minister and he has not answered it. He asked where the money will come from to do the wonderful things proposed by members of the opposition. We have told him where the money would come from but the question is rightfully put to the Minister of Finance: Where will he get the money to pay for the ever-increasing welfare rolls?

April 22, 1993
Supply
In Prince George, the major community in my riding, I took the time to look at this situation. If we are going to address these problems we have to know what we are dealing with. In Prince George alone there are some
5,000	people on social assistance. A number of those people are not able to work and will likely never work. In our country where we measure our value by how well we take care of those who are less well off-my colleague from Trinity-Spadina said that better than I did-we clearly have to continue to help those people.
Government has to initiate projects for training but the private sector also has a responsibility. It is not often mentioned in this House because our natural inclination as members of Parliament is to look at the role of government. There is a role and a responsibility for the private sector as well. On matters of research and development and innovation we have some winners in this country, but it is also clear that the private sector has failed Canada in a number of areas as well.
There are reasons for that, such as the branch plant economy we have in Canada and the seemingly endless reliance on being the hewers of wood and drawers of water. We must take advantage of existing legislation and programs to ensure that we do get an opportunity to add value to those wood products in particular-I am interested in that for my riding-and other similar areas. We do have some tools at hand that we can use.
I realize that I only have a few minutes left but one particular example sums this up. In my riding of Prince George-Bulkley Valley I have met with the workers at the Kelly Douglas & Co. warehouse and corresponded with the company owners. This warehouse has been in operation for many years in Prince George. It closed virtually overnight and some 65 people were laid off. A number of them had done nothing else in their lives. They had worked full time in that particular warehouse at good pay but now they were unemployed. The workers have said that the local management was treated as poorly as they had been treated. So what do we do? What does the union do? What does the company do?
This is the classic situation of a good leadership role being played by the union and a poorer role being played
by the company. There are also some serious questions about what to do in our economy.
In this particular case the union has taken a leadership role by working with its members who used to work at this warehouse. It contacted the Canada Employment Centre and is now working with these people-some have done no other work in their lives-to prepare them and help them look for other work. I visited the classroom where they are beii.g trained to prepare resumes and introduced to computers. One person said: "Well, this is fine. I appreciate being involved in this class, but why are the taxpayers paying for this?" I thought he had a good question there. He suggested that the employer should be paying more attention to these workers now that they have been laid off. The union is challenging what this particular company is doing as well through a grievance procedure.
This is the classic situation of the seemingly uncaring employer, but it is also a unique situation because the union has gone far beyond its traditional role and is working to serve its members. There is an increasing concentration of business in larger and larger centres where communities like the ones I represent have fewer and fewer services.
After raising those challenges from that very specific example I now come to some positive solutions and suggestions and, most important, some choices. I want to impress on anyone who is watching this debate, earnestly concerned about the state of our country's finances and eagerly waiting to see what the Finance Minister does with his budget on Monday, that there are some choices. The New Democrats and in particular our leader have made some effort to develop our strategy for a full employment economy. We have met the challenge of presenting alternatives. This is a reasonable plan. It has been given the rubber stamp of approval from independent financial consultants. It can be done. There is a different way of running the economy rather than this government's approach. There are positive solutions that give people meaningful jobs and the opportunity to present and participate in economic planning.
I encourage anyone who is interested in that debate to please write to us. We will send them a copy of it. Then they can certainly get a chance to see what the alternative is and what the challenges and choices are.
April 22, 1993

Mr. Speaker, we are discussing a very important topic today, the economy. In my neck of the woods, forestry is a major part of the economy and we have been hit quite hard. I know the hon. member representing his party has the responsibility of following the forestry sector for his party. I know he is quite knowledgeable in that area.
I would like to mention to the House that in my area of Restigouche-Chaleur there is a mill in Atholville, New Brunswick that has been closed. We have another mill in Dalhousie that has been closed 50 per cent. Two of its four machines have been closed down. I have been quite concerned about the policies of this government with regard to high interest rates, the high dollar and its effect on industry and more specifically on the forestry industry. I have also been concerned about other policies.
I wonder if the hon. member would care to comment about the policies of this government with regard to the forestry industry.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the question from the member. We have sat on a number of committees and discussed the concerns of the forestry sector in the country.
He is quite right when he mentions a range of problems and issues facing the forestry sector. We know the challenges faced by all governments and in particular provincial governments that are faced with the day-today management of the allocation of the forest resource to companies. There is a clear challenge there on the question of set-asides and meeting the goals of the Brundtland commission for 12 per cent. That difficult challenge is particular to my own province of British Columbia and is a very important one. It is important to mention on this Earth Day that it is a very difficult time for most provincial governments.
With regard to the high dollar and in particular trade policy, I would just like to comment on two things. The general approach to the high interest rates and the high dollar has been very difficult and has hurt all components of our forestry sector, particularly as it relates to our exports to the United States.
Supply
Of course I must mention the softwood lumber tariff dispute that we have had with the United States. We anticipate a ruling next week from GATT that is discussing the whole subsidy question. This whole issue of the current tariff and what is to be expected is before a couple of panels now and is hanging over the forestry sector. The U.S. lumber lobby has already said that if it loses at any one of these panels it will be launching an extraordinary challenge to the decision, so the whole dispute over softwood lumber is nowhere near finished yet.
One of the problems in eastern Canada is the age of our mills and particularly a lot of the pulp mills. The owners are having difficulty making those very big money decisions about reinvestment into those mills. There is upgrading necessary to improve the water treatment systems of those mills. As one of the most important sectors in Canada there is a great deal more to do.
I am wondering, on the eve of the budget, if we are going to see a forestry minister continue in this House. There has been some debate in the government about doing away with the minister. It would be ironic since one of the first pieces of legislation my colleague and I worked on when we arrived in Parliament was the creation of that department. If one of the last actions of this government was to do away with that department in such an important sector I do not think most Canadians would appreciate it.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to join in today's debate concerning the state of the Canadian economy.
I would like to respond to a few of the comments made by previous speakers. I think we should not allow all of them to go unchallenged, especially when they may have left an inappropriate or incorrect impression.
It is fair to say that every member of this House would prefer an economy that was stronger with more employment, more jobs and higher incomes. Of course, that would benefit not just the people with those jobs, it would also benefit governments. It would benefit governments because people with jobs earn income and pay taxes. Fewer of them would be drawing on the govern-

April 22, 1993
Supply
merit's social programs, such as unemployment insurance or welfare. Governments would be receiving revenues. That would make life a lot easier for them in trying to control the deficit which all levels of government are now having a great amount of difficulty in doing. We would like to have the revenues from those higher taxes both from individuals and from corporations with profits.
It is fair to say that all of us would be interested in having a stronger economy. The real question is as to what degree can government action produce that stronger economy.
Unfortunately what has happened in the last few years is that we have become unable to be insulated from events in the rest of the world. It used to be, probably since the end of the Second World War until the mid-1970s, that as a country we were able to set ourselves aside and avoid a lot of the economic factors which had great influence, at many times negative, in other parts of the world. In part, that was because we had a lot of natural resources on which we could rely and we were able to determine our own force and set our own agenda. We had high income and high value from those resources. For example, that is why we were able to insulate ourselves in many ways from the oil price shock of the early 1970s. We did not have to endure what many European countries or Japan had to endure, for example the high prices of energy which harmed or had a great impact on their economies.
The fact of the matter is in today's world we no longer have that insulation. Today's world is a multinational trading world. Goods and services trade throughout the world. Modem communications and computers have meant that manufacturing jobs can be shifted to what used to be Third World countries. Those countries now compete with us for jobs that we used to consider as our own and natural to Canada. The fact is that we no longer have the luxury of saying that in Canada we will set our own course regardless of what the rest of the world does.
One of the comments made earlier in the debate concerned interest rates and the high dollar. One of the things that causes the dollar to be stronger or higher against other currencies is borrowing money in foreign currencies and bringing it to Canada. The prime borrowers in foreign currencies and foreign markets are governments or government agencies.
It is not the federal government that has resorted to that. It is provincial governments such as the Government of Ontario. The Government of Ontario, and add to that Ontario Hydro, its Crown-owned agency producing electric power in that province, is probably the most substantive borrower of funds outside of Canada. The current NDP government is continuing the practice that was established by other governments at an even higher rate than ever before. When those governments borrow in foreign currencies, naturally those currencies are converted into Canadian currency when they are going to pay for goods and services in Canada. That increases the value of our dollar which is something that has been complained about by the opposition.
When governments borrow money either domestically or from foreigners, that borrowing puts pressure on the amount of capital available for investment and for other purposes which raises interest rates. When we have complaints from the opposition members about the level of interest rates or about the level of the dollar, I encourage them to look at what is behind these figures and what is causing it. To the extent that government is responsible, it is government spending and government deficits. The people of Canada have become increasingly concerned about those deficits. I think and I hope that in his budget next week the Minister of Finance will present once again an updated and credible plan to deal with that.
Earlier a member of the Liberal Party suggested that we have paid for many of these difficulties and we are continuing to pay. Unfortunately, that is true. Unfortunately over a period of time, for 10 or 15 years, as governments, and I will restrict this to the federal government for the moment, we increased our expenditures at 10 per cent to 15 per cent per year for 15 years. That went on until about 1984. It built a debt in this country of something in the order of $200 billion. For the period of 1975 to 1985 the debt increased 10 times what it had been.
April 22, 1993

Since then the current government has tried to control that spending. We have kept spending below the rate of inflation, in the neighbourhood of 3 per cent to 4 per cent per year average over that time. We have tried to control the deficit. There have been increases in taxes, there is no question about that. In spite of that, the interest on the debt that was there in 1984 has continued to accumulate and that has brought the current debt in this period to approximately $400 billion. It has almost doubled. That has happened simply because we have seen interest on that existing debt.
It is a rule of thumb when investment counsellors are talking to people, counselling them on saving money and saving for their future that if money is put away, if money is invested and saved today, that roughly in seven years that money will double. Unfortunately from the other point of view, if there is a debt today which is not paid, in seven years that debt will be approximately double. That is what has happened over the last period of time. It is not because this current government has gone on a spending spree and spent more money.
We have found ways to provide the programs we felt most necessary through restructuring and eliminating some of the programs and some of the spending that we felt we could do without. On every single occasion we did that, we were opposed by the opposition parties.
I can mention one example. We started with a post office that had a deficit of $600 million a year. It was costing Canadian taxpayers $600 million a year. That post office is currently either making a small profit or breaking even. We have turned it around from a loss of $600 million a year to roughly a break-even or small profit situation. Why has that happened? It has happened for a couple reasons. It has happened because in that business we have adopted new technology, new methods of service to people. We have changed the strategy and the focus and we have brought it into the modem age.
Unfortunately in Canada some people seem to suggest that we can continue to maintain industries in the face of international competition, in the face of changing technologies and in the face of new products and services that have come to replace some of the ways we used to do things. We cannot remain locked in the past. I think everyone understands that. I think even everyone who
Supply
worked in the factories that were talked about earlier where those factories have for one reason or another closed would agree that in part it is because we have not found new technology or invested in new technology in those areas to make ourselves competitive with the rest of the world. As I said earlier, we no longer have the luxury of being non-competitive.
We had some good comments earlier by the hon. member for Willowdale when he talked about the need for investment in technology and for investment in research and development. There is no question about that. We all understand that. The question is that in order to make that, we have to free up that investment for research and development, for investment in new technology that will make our workers and business more productive. We must not crowd that investment out by continuing to increase government spending and government borrowing on current consumption. That is very difficult because we have a lot of demand for the services of government.
We can see the difficulty in provincial governments. There were comments a moment ago from members of the New Democratic Party. However we have a New Democratic government in Ontario. Ontario is 43 per cent of the Canadian economy. If the methods being suggested here today by the New Democratic Party were successful and worked, it should have the strongest economy. We should have a booming economy right now.
We know that the Rae government tried those in the first two years it was in office. It was a disaster and it has admitted now that it was on the wrong course. The treasurer, Mr. Laughren, and the premier, Mr. Rae, have been saying in recent days that they are going to have to change course, adopt a different fiscal plan, reduce their spending and reduce their deficit because they can no longer continue on the path on which they have put themselves.
They have recognized it. The NDP have recognized the folly of the kind of thinking they continue to perpetuate in this House. They have recognized it in Ontario because they ran up against the wall. They ran up against people saying: "No, we are not going to lend more money. If you want to borrow you are going to have

April 22, 1993
Supply
to pay either excessive interest rates or we are not going to lend it to you at all". That reality has brought the fact home to the NDP government in Ontario that it is going to have to adopt a different strategy. What strategy is it adopting? It is adopting a strategy that this government has been conducting for several years.
One can say that we are not particularly happy with the level of unemployment or the state of the economy. I can say that I am not happy. But the question we have to ask is: If we had not adopted the policies that we have been pursuing over the last few years, where would we be?
For example, there was talk earlier about trade. Trade is the life-blood of this country. We depend on trade for about one-third of our income. We have to do everything we can to remain competitive so that we can continue to trade in the world and compete against goods and services from the rest of the world and increase our exports.
In 1992 exports reached a record high level of $157 billion. That was 11 per cent above 1991. Exports to the United States reached a record high level of $122 billion. That was $19 billion more than in 1988. That is under the free trade agreement. Under the free trade agreement we have increased exports by $20 billion, about 20 per cent since 1988, to the United States. There has been an increase of 10 per cent from 1991 in the over-all exports to the world. Our exports to Japan for example increased from 1984 to 1992 by over 40 per cent, to a record level of $16 billion. Why is that? It is because we have been pursuing trade opportunities such as the free trade agreement. It is also because we have been removing impediments regarding Canadian businesses and their ability to trade.
Someone mentioned the GST briefly in this debate. That was one of the most difficult policies for this government and for members like myself who supported that policy to go out into the country, to tell people, to explain to people why we had to make this change. We told people why we had to eliminate a federal sales tax that was hidden and buried in the cost of our products, that was crippling our manufacturers' ability to produce products and trade in the world or to compete against imports. We told them why we had to eliminate that tax and instead replace it with a new tax called the GST. We had the courage to do that.
We heard earlier about the Canadian Manufacturers' Association. Somehow it was suggested that we are not supporting some initiative of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association. There was no stronger supporter of the GST than the Canadian Manufacturers' Association. We supported that, we eliminated the federal sales tax, we put in a new tax called the GST and this was very difficult politically. No one knows better than I.
I had town hall meetings in my riding. Many, many people came to those meetings. In many cases they were very angry people. They were opposed to the government doing this. They argued instead that we should be cutting government spending by that amount.
However, cutting spending by that amount would have required us to be cutting payments for example to senior citizens and others. We said no, we will have to replace this tax with another tax called the GST and we did it. We did it in spite of that political difficulty because we had the courage to do it.
What has happened? Our exporters have become more competitive. We see that in the numbers we are showing.
People talked about high interest rates. High interest rates are driven by inflation and government spending. We have been keeping government spending under control, not as well as we would have liked, but that has not been the problem.
It is revenue that has fallen short because of the weakness in the domestic and world economies. The Canadian economy has not been as strong as we would have hoped. Therefore government revenues are approximately $10 billion a year less than what we were expecting. This has put enormous pressure on us.
However, the policies we have pursued, such as the elimination of the federal sales tax to replace it with the GST and the introduction of the free trade agreements and others, have put us in a position where currently we are one of the stronger economies in the world. We should recognize that.
It is not a situation where we are totally insulated or when we can simply say that in Canada we will have our economy and we will ignore what is going on in the rest of the world.
April 22, 1993

In terms of the G-7 nations, Canada is expected to lead the world. The OECD says that among its larger members Canada has made the greatest progress in recent years in reducing its structural deficit.
Without the government's actions to control its spending, the deficit would have reached $82 billion by 1991-92, which is close to two and one half times the actual level. The debt would have reached $645 billion.
In spite of the fact that we have not made the progress that we would have liked, certainly that I would have liked, we have made some of the greatest progress in recent years in the OECD, the 24 industrial nations of the world.
In terms of the future world economy, the OECD forecast in its most recent global outlook that Canada will be the leader among the world's seven largest economies in 1993-94.
If all our policies were wrong and if all the things that we did in the last seven or eight years were incorrect, why would our competitors, the OECD and our Canadian forecasters such as the Royal Bank last week and the C.D. Howe Institute and others be saying that Canada is now expected to be one of the world's leading economies in the next few years?
The reason for that is because we had the courage to do the things that needed to be done. Everybody understood that these things were difficult. Everybody understood that it is difficult for a government to say no, we are not going to continue to spend money like $600 million a year subsidizing the post office or $600 million a year subsidizing VIA Rail when nobody takes that service.
We made those difficult decisions. They were decisions at the time that were difficult for me because I had to defend them among my constituents. Having made them, we have now reached a point where we have the lowest inflation in 30 years.
Inflation is virtually non-existent. We have the lowest interest rates seen in probably 30 years. We have interest rates and mortgage rates that have been unheard of. One can get a mortgage now for under 6 per cent. One has to go back to 1962 to find a time when one could get a mortgage for under 6 per cent.
These are the policies that were long-term policies. They were policies that put in place an environment and a structure in Canada through which we could look to
Supply
long-term growth. They are not policies where we simply borrow more money and spend it today.
Yes, we might be able to borrow some money and spend it. It might create a few jobs. However, tomorrow when we try to pay that money back, just like we have the problem now in paying for the borrowing we already made, we will have a weakened economy. It weakens our ability as a government to respond to problems.
I will end now. I look forward to the questions that may come to me. I think we have put in place the policies that will secure our future. What we need now is to continue them and not to change them.

Mr. Speaker, I was intrigued by the mental gymnastics of the member opposite and the suggestion that perhaps what the rest of the country is witnessing is a misperception of some great economic strategy that is being actually foisted upon us for our benefit.
There was the question of the benefit that Canadians are receiving for some of the very courageous decisions that the government made over the course of the last nine years. I wonder if this would include the fact that the government has had the temerity to visit upon us over the course of the last two years the following number of bankruptcies: 11,180 in 1990, 12,952 in 1991 and 13,851 in 1992. This is all for a relative value of $2.8 billion, $4.9 billion and $5.5 billion. This is a real good economic strategy.
He said: "We had to make some real tough decisions in terms of taxation. We brought in taxation because we wanted to decrease the deficit and reduce the debt". However, he acknowledged that the debt has gone up to in excess of $400 billion, over 100 per cent since the Tories took office. The deficit has not been measurably decreased even though personal income taxes have gone up by over 74 per cent over the course of the last eight years.
Except for the rich.

That is right. Except for those who can afford to pay it.
He has also ignored the fact that part of the economic package has seen for example that the trade balance in this country upon which a great portion of our wealth depends has gone from a positive value of $19.8 billion

April 22, 1993
Supply
in 1984 when these great sages of economic planning came in to a bare $9.4 billion last year.
When we take a look at the current account balance the difference is much more seriously negative. In fact the current account balance went from a positive value of $3,457 billion in 1984 to a net deficit of $28,563 billion last year.
I want to know what the courageous decisions actually are that this government made. The hon. member talks about the GST but that did not require great courage. It required great stupidity. This is only if we believe the figures that the government gives us. It will have to require a great leap of faith on our part, given the record. If we take a look at the figures the government gives us on the GST it says we had a net return of roughly $.5 billion last year. That compares with the $18.5 billion MST that it was getting before the GST was brought in.
The other figures that the government gave us is that it collected $30 billion and gave back roughly $14.5 billion. Of that $30 billion, $9 billion was collected on imports. There is an increase of over 100 per cent in the GST or sales tax revenue on imports and $20 billion on domestic items with over half of it given back in rebates and refunds.
What it tells us is that either the government does not have a grasp of the impact of its taxation and it has driven the economy underground or it has taxed the economy into non-existence, as witnessed by the large rate of bankruptcies and the volume in both numbers and dollars of the value of those bankruptcies.
Because we are all reasonable men and women in this House, could we please, through you, Mr. Speaker, get an explanation from the member opposite of where this courage is to be manifested and where the benefits of that courage can be seen for those of us Canadians who witnessed a 75 per cent increase in income taxes and a whole array of other tax increases? My colleagues tell me that there were in excess of 35 tax increases during its administration. Would he be so good as to explain to those of us who are paying for the tune just what kind of music we should be listening to?

Mr. Speaker, it is interesting that we have a member from the Liberal Party speaking about taxes and spending when in fact he suggested that we have a debt that is now approximately twice what it was eight years ago. I acknowledged that earlier. The fact of the matter is that in the previous eight years the Liberal government took the debt and increased it by 10 times. Not only that, let us take a look at where that debt was in 1984. All of the debt that has accumulated since that time is interest on that debt that we inherited.
Over the period of time between then and now we have successfully run this government in the black. We have also been able to pay some money toward that debt that we inherited. We are now in a position, having established a government that runs in the black, to say: "Can we attack that debt and that deficit". This is because, as we know, the longer it goes unpaid, the more the interest accumulates and the bigger the amount we have to pay. That is what we are talking about doing and that is what the Minister of Finance will talk about doing in his budget next week. I think all Canadians recognize that.
I think all Canadians recognize that we can no longer continue on the path that we were put on by the Liberal government. They recognize that we have turned that around. They recognize that we are paying our way as we go now and that we have to now attack the debt that they left us before it accumulates even more interest, which accumulates every single day.
That member should be apologizing for putting this country in that position. It has taken us this long and all this pain and difficulty to get back to a point now where we find ourselves among the countries, as was just mentioned earlier, that can look forward to the highest growth, the strongest economy and the most employment growth among the G-7 countries.

Mr. Speaker, I listened carefully to the hon. member during his remarks and I noticed that at one point he attributed the problems of Canadian exports to the fact that some of our industries have been allowed to fall behind in the development of their productivity.
Had the member been here earlier perhaps he would have heard my colleague, the hon. member for Essex- Windsor, point out that the GM foundry plant in
April 22, 1993

St. Catharines is rated the most efficient foundry plant on the continent and that its wage level is $9 an hour below the equivalent foundry plant wage levels in the United States.
How can the member account for the shutting down now by GM of that foundry plant on the basis of a lack of efficiency and how can he argue that it is not on the basis of the free trade agreement?

Mr. Speaker, I have to confess to not being particularly familiar with the foundry plant in St. Catharines. However, I would say that if it is as efficient as the member suggests, if it is as competitive as the member suggests then I am sure that there is somebody out there who would be more than interested in acquiring this plant and operating it because it sounds to me like it would be very profitable.
It is very unusual for companies or owners of plants to close them down when they are profitable. I would like to hear from the member, if he has an opportunity to tell me, if this is a profitable plant. If it is then I can probably find a buyer.

Mr. Speaker, it is my intent to share my time today with one of my colleagues. We rise to speak on this opposition motion that this House condemn the government for policies that have decimated the economy and forced company closures, resulting in job losses for Canadian workers. I want to stress the decimation that has occurred in our resource sector in related industries under this administration.
Canada has been identified by the United Nations as the best country in the world in which to live and yet in the last nine years under this administration we have seen our national debt increase to more than $450 billion. Our current account deficit at the end of the last fiscal year was $28.5 billion and the budget deficit is out of control. Unemployment is at an all-time high with 1.5 million Canadians unemployed.
What is even more serious as far as I am concerned is that our resources are being depleted by interests outside Canada. If we were in any other business these depleted inventories would have to be deducted from the value of the business or company. This government gives no such accounting of the depletion of Canada's re-
Supply
sources and I suggest such an accounting is urgently required as we note what is happening here in Canada.
This government is more interested in its image in other countries than it is in the well-being of the Canadian people and the Canadian economy. As we examine the resource industry in Canada, we are blessed with tremendous resources but we note that the Atlantic fisheries industry has been decimated due to overfishing by foreign interests. Only after the stocks have been depleted by the factory trawler ships has the government decided to take a hard line and force realistic cutbacks. In the meantime, thousands upon thousands of Canadians have been forced out of the industry and are now on unemployment and social assistance.
We have witnessed the hardships in the forestry industry that is only now beginning to recover. Harvesting methods such as clear-cutting are environmental disasters but are practised in the name of efficiency.
The Canadian food industry is being traded away by an uncaring government and its incompetent negotiators who have utterly failed to realize the impact across rural Canada. This impact has created untold hardships on thousands of Canadian producers in the agricultural industry in the towns and villages across this nation who provide the services to the primary producers.
I submit to this House of Commons, to this highest court of the land that we as Canadians must establish rules to control our resources, the processing of these resources and the environment. Otherwise this plundering by the transnational companies that have no loyalties to this nation will destroy our resource base, our industry and our standard of living that has been the envy of other nations. We as Canadians must put a stop to this madness immediately. We must put an end to the current trend of governing by corporate decision and above all we must take back control of this country. In the next six months Canadians will have the opportunity to make that decision and I am confident they will respond with the future of Canada first and foremost in their minds.
Let me just put on the record again in this House the number of food processing plants that have been closed or forced out of business since January 1989 when the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement came into effect. There have been 107 plant closings or major lay-offs. This government is obviously going to force the NAFTA legislation through the House, regardless of the lack of support by the Canadian people and regardless of

April 22, 1993
Supply
whether or not it is going to pass the United States Congress. This government is going to sacrifice our Canadian workers, our environmental standards, our food quality and our resources in return for access to a foreign market for telecommunications, banking and financial institutions.
Let me give just a few of the facts and figures on the increases of vegetable imports into Canada between 1990 and 1992. Canned tomatoes increased by 85 per cent; tomato paste, 33 per cent; canned tomatoes, 191 per cent; canned peas, 250 per cent; baby carrots, 2,400 per cent; carrots and peas mixed, 2,900 per cent; canned beets, 87 per cent and tomato sauces, 873 per cent, an increase from 3,515 tonnes to 30,699 tonnes. The trade tribunal did not see any damage to our economy. This is nonsense. One company that discontinued canning tomatoes, peas and pumpkins is now importing large quantities of canned products from the U.S. and only the labelling is done in Canada. This company will be importing up to 92,000 cartons of processed pumpkin alone by the end of June 1993.
All these vegetables were previously grown in Canada and provided income for Canadian farmers, service industries and workers. Now they are being grown in another country where input costs and wages are lower.
We appear to have lost a market for our Canadian corn to be processed into breakfast foods. We have seen the meat packing plants, the flour mills and the pickle plants close. The list goes on and on.
We are told we must be globally competitive but as I have previously stated in this House, the global competition is a few huge transnational corporations whose loyalties are bottom line profits to uncaring shareholders in other countries.
Let me put on the record the devastation that has occurred. I want to cite an example from a news article written by Hugh Zimmer of Otterville, Ontario, a recognized writer and researcher. He points out that everyone ignores the Mexican labour issue. The regulations are ignored. The underground economy is estimated at 25 per cent of the labour force. The plan is
similar to cheaper Portugal being used to lure jobs away from areas of Europe with higher wages.
How can any government in Canada with any conscience be part of such an arrangement that will undermine our structures and our standard of living, unless it is acting on behalf of these corporations that have no loyalties to this nation?
Mexican labour rates decreased dramatically from 1979 to 1989. We know their environmental standards do not measure up to ours. We know their food processing standards do not measure up to ours. The use of pesticides, herbicides and other chemicals used in food production and processing is not as stringent as in Canada. My research shows that of 48 chemicals used in food production and processing in Mexico, 12 are banned in Canada.
Before going into a trade agreement with any nation or nations, these nations should either measure up to our standards or, under article III of the GAIT, their products should not be allowed access to our markets. To do otherwise is a betrayal of trust to Canadian businesses, Canadian workers and Canadian consumers whose health could well be impacted on by these lower standards.
Canadian agriculture and food production simply cannot survive with such declining returns and the increased input costs we have in Canada versus those of other nations.
As food production and processing on this planet falls under the control of fewer and fewer corporations, we see the government members acting like a herd of lemmings heading for self-destruction. They lack the courage and backbone to place Canadian interests first.
Our workers are responsible, our environmental standards are reasonable, but they are being sacrificed in the name of global competitiveness based on lower standards in other countries.
I ask the Minister of Finance when he presents his budget next Monday to include measures to ensure that Canada's resource industries will be put back under the control of Canadian interests. Measures must be taken to ensure the long-term prosperity of this nation and put a stop to the plundering that will eventually destroy Canada.
April 22, 1993

I want to put on record one of the things I recently saw. In Benchmark, Ontario a cash crop farm with 80 per cent equity and a net cash income of $47,000 in 1987, government payments of $25,251 over the next five years, decreased by 30 per cent. Expenses increased by $12,000. In 1987 returns from the operation exceeded operating expenses by $22,000. In 1992 this situation reversed and operating expenses exceeded market returns by $8,000.
This situation cannot be allowed to continue. The same situation exists in Saskatchewan and other provinces across Canada. I submit that we as Canadians have to take control of our economy, our natural resources and our food processing. We must maintain our health and environmental standards and, above all, the standards that apply to our workers.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans is leaving fishermen in Nova Scotia on the hook. For literally months the minister has been promising there would be a federal compensation package to support communities in eastern Nova Scotia devastated by the quota cuts.
It is now April 22 and there still has been no announcement. A task force from the Nova Scotia provincial government proposed a plan to the minister well over a month ago.
Perhaps the real reason behind this inordinate delay is so the government can announce this package in the midst of the provincial election to help the rapidly fading
government of Don Cameron and the provincial Conservative Party.
I wish to inform this House that if the minister and the federal Conservative Party are using Nova Scotia fishermen as election bait they will not get their votes. Stop the politics, stop this cynical manoeuvring and start helping those people who need the government's help the most and who need it now.

Mr. Speaker, Canada's forestry industry is on the rebound. In the first nine months of 1992 pulp production was up 20 per cent and lumber production was up by 13 per cent. With the recent surge in lumber prices, 1993 promises to be a good year.
I would like to congratulate forestry companies in Alberta for investing approximately $2.7 billion and creating 1,700 jobs in this sector of our economy this year.
This industry is poised for growth. This growth is targeted to foreign markets. This government is committed to promoting access for Canadian products into foreign markets through the free trade agreement, the GATT and the NAFTA.

Mr. Speaker, Oxfam Canada has been advised that the Canadian International Development Agency has arbitrarily decided not to participate in phase two of the Canada-Na-mibia co-operation agreement. CIDA worked with Oxfam Canada to design this five-year Century Focus project which was to spend about $7 million in Namibia, 10 per cent from Oxfam and 90 per cent from CIDA. The CIDA contribution represented Canada's bilateral aid to the newest member of the Commonwealth of Nations.
Namibia is a success story and a point of hope on the African continent. The cuts in foreign aid are unacceptable everywhere, but where a country has finally been nurtured from oppression to democracy Canada is doubly wrong for so quickly abandoning this fledgling nation.

April 22, 1993
The preoccupation with eastern Europe will be a tragedy if it means that we desert or even betray our earlier commitments. I call on the government to reverse this decision or at least wait until the first phase can be evaluated.

Mr. Speaker, April has been declared Parkinson Awareness Month. Parkinson's disease is the second largest neurodegenerative disease in Canada. One person in 200 over the age of 40 and one person in 100 over the age of 55 may develop this chemical disorder of the brain. Since 1965 the Parkinson Foundation of Canada has been striving to help people with Parkinson's disease. It raises funds for research, provides information and counselling services to patients, their families and caregivers, and raises public awareness through various activities.
Activities for Parkinson Awareness Month will vary from chapter to chapter. One beautiful symbol of the struggle against Parkinson's disease is the red and white Dr. James Parkinson tulip named for the physician who first described the symptoms of this disease.
Please join with me in wishing the Parkinson Foundation of Canada and its many volunteers a very successful Parkinson Awareness Month.

Mr. Speaker, today we celebrate Earth Day with tree planting and environmental events across the country. As individuals and as a country we must take responsibility for leaving future generations a healthy planet.
Many Canadians take actions to protect the environment but expect governments at all levels to do what citizens alone cannot do. For instance, we have to work to eliminate pollution and prevent toxic chemicals from entering the air, soil, rivers and lakes. We have to stop overfishing and protect the ocean habitat. We have to harvest our forests carefully and conserve old growth forests. We need legislation to protect endangered plants and animals. We need to use energy more efficiently and produce a national plan to prevent global warming. We should help the poor in securing adequate nourishment, shelter and health standards.
In other words, we have a lot to do and so little time. Let us make every day Earth Day.

subtopic: EUROPEAN BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
EUROPEAN BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadians are outraged at the fact that their hard-earned tax dollars are being purposely squandered by the president of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, Mr. Jacques Attali.
His personal Napoleonic pipe-dream of Taj Mahal-like grandeur for EBRD headquarters fundamentally mocks the good intentions and compassion with which Canadians contributed.
The purpose of this bank was to use the vast majority of its funds for the creation and development of private sector businesses and market economies in the former Communist regimes.
I, and I am sure Canadians everywhere, applaud the efforts of our representative at the bank, Mr. Donald McCutchan. Mr. McCutchan, courageously, was the only bank board member to vote no to this breach of trust.
I call upon this government, despite today's apology by Mr. Attali, to strengthen its determination to rectify this mess and get on with the rebuilding of eastern Europe.

Mr. Speaker, on Saturday, April 24, the entire world will remember the first holocaust of the 20th century.
Armenian Canadians will be on Parliament Hill at 12.30 p.m. to pray and remind humanity of the horror of those years of suffering.
My colleague and friend, the hon. member for Gatineau-La Lievre, along with many other members of Parliament, will give our fellow citizens the assurance of
April 22, 1993

our active commitment to have this event proclaimed by Canada and to take up this issue to the UN.
Sunday evening, in Montreal, I will be present at one of the Armenian churches Sourp Hagop, and I invite all my colleagues to attend.

Mr. Speaker, 50 years ago in the Warsaw ghetto courageous Jewish resistance fighters were in their third day of a desperate 27-day battle against overwhelming Nazi forces.
This weekend I will join my community in commemorating the 78th anniversary of the Armenian genocide which was the model for the Nazi holocaust.
Don Valley North is home to many people who have experienced racist and/or religious violence. There are also many people who have risked their lives in wars combating these evils which humiliate, hurt and destroy so many innocent people.
Canadians must remember and our children must be taught these horrendous lessons of the past. We must resolve to continue to fight for human rights and freedom from discrimination in Canada and around the world.

Today, Mr. Speaker, hundreds of young students and their parents are here on Parliament Hill to protest the unfair budget cuts the Ontario New Democratic government is imposing on De La Salle High School.
At stake is the unique program offered at the De La Salle Centre for artistic excellence; this program is the only one of its kind in Ontario to serve the numerous artistic needs of our French-speaking youth.
It is imperative that the people should let the New Democratic Premier of Ontario know how crucial it is to restore the level of financing so that our young people
can mature and develop their talents to join the ranks of the Canadian arts community.
There are 17 English schools in Ontario offering similar arts programs to serve the needs of the majority. Just one school in the whole province of Ontario to serve half a million young French-speaking Ontarians, is that too much to ask?
I invite all French-speaking Canadians and their friends to write to the Ontario premier telling him that francophones in his province are asking no more but no less than what the majority enjoys.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for External Relations; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today is Earth Day. On this occasion, I am proud to say that, in its various policies and programs, Canada has made every effort possible to live up to the commitments made by our Prime Minister at the Earth Summit in Rio.
Our country has taken part in several international initiatives designed to preserve our natural environment.
For example, CIDA manages Canada's contribution to the launching of the experimental stage of the Global Environment Facility and has established a very innovative program designed to assist Canadian companies in making their most advanced environmental technology available to developing countries.
As agreed at that Summit, CIDA is playing a leadership role in the preparations for an international convention on desertification.
In closing, I would like to invite all Canadian men and women to ponder upon those questions and ask themselves what contribution they can make to the preservation of our planet.

Mr. Speaker, on March 19 I rose in this House and asked how this Conservative government could allow mass reclassification of senior bureaucrats while refusing the legitimate

April 22, 1993
reclassification of fisheries officers and marine surveyors.
The labour minister assured me that the President of the Treasury Board would respond to me as soon as he came back to the House. That was a month ago and there has not been a word.
In the meantime the government's classification grievance committee has ruled that the reclassification of fisheries assistant deputy supervisors is less important than that of a government interior designer because the designer's decisions affect the projected image of Canada as well as the resources of the department.
Do fisheries assistant deputy supervisors, and in fact marine surveyors, not affect the projected image of Canada as well as the resources of the department? What about the safety hazards they face?
This is not about reclassification. This is about paying off senior bureaucrats with wage increases at a time of across the board wage freezes, and this government's total unwillingness to provide legitimate reclassification of fisheries officers and marine surveyors.

Mr. Speaker, I rise in the House of Commons today to remember the Armenian genocide that began on April 24, 1915.
I know that my colleagues in the House agree on the importance of remembering this day and mourning the loss of 1.5 million people who were killed in this horrific massacre. We must not lose sight of the impact this tremendous loss of life has had on the Armenian people. They were the daughters and sons, mothers and fathers, and wives and husbands of a nation of Armenian people who perished in this brutal extermination.
The tragedy is that Canada and most countries in the world have not officially recognized the 1915 massacre as a genocide.

Mr. Speaker, almost half of all Canadians volunteer their time and energy to a worthy cause at some point in their lives.
National Volunteer Week reminds us that these individuals make a vital contribution to our families and communities. It also provides an opportunity to recognize the efforts of special organizations, many of which would cease to exist without the commitment of their volunteers.
Calgary has been called the most active volunteer city in Canada. As the member representing Calgary North I can testify to the fact that our city is second to none in this regard.
The Family Life Education Council, Kids First, the YWCA, the Schizophrenia Association of Alberta and the many community organizations in Calgary are only a few that come to mind when I think of community builders which rely on volunteers. These organizations know first hand that volunteers represent the heart and soul of their operation. They also know there is no limit to what people can accomplish when they work together toward a common goal.
I would like to express sincere thanks to those individuals and organizations who contribute daily to our families and our communities. Their efforts make a world of difference.
I challenge everyone to get involved with the revitalization of our community as volunteers.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George-Bulkley Valley):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last December GATT ruled that the United States had the right to use special procedures to launch a countervail action against Canada's softwood lumber exports.
GATT also ruled that the $15 million in bonds that were collected by the U.S. government should be returned to Canadian companies.
The GATT subsidies committee meets next week to deal with this ongoing dispute and the government
April 22, 1993

should be monitoring this matter closely for the many communities across the country that depend on the forest industry.
The minister said he would be aggressive with the Americans to get our money back. The minister should tell the House how much money the Americans have returned to us.
In other words, we want our money back. Rather than kowtowing to the U.S. all the time this government should be prepared to defend Canadian exports and Canadian jobs.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government of Canada and the Canadian Seed Growers' Association are pleased to recognize the appointment of two outstanding seed growers to the Order of Canada.
They are Mr. Leonard Haney of Picture Butte, Alberta and Mr. Harvey Gjesdal of Birch Hills, Saskatchewan. Both gentlemen are credited with recognized excellence in their respective fields of production, pedigreed seed.
These two gentlemen have given a lifetime of performance to the seed industry of Canada and to agriculture in Canada. They have helped producers across this nation, received achievements for producing top of the line quality products of grains and oilseeds and have enabled Canada to be in a position to better serve the world by feeding the world and to take our proper place.
I ask the House to congratulate these two accomplished agriculture producers.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, two consecutive Secretaries of State have failed to bring forward a student loans program that is revitalized and responds to the needs of Canadian students.
Here is what has to be done if they have been listening to Canadians. Remove the 3 per cent tax on student
Oral Questions
loans and cut the additional six months' interest. Involve students in the student loan criteria if it must be given to the banks. Have flexible loans that respond to part-time students and variable workloads and increase the criteria for loans. They have not been changed since 1984.
If those in government want more help, I am willing to give it to them.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Acting Prime Minister.
Last night we learned of yet another Somalia shooting, allegedly at the hands of Canadian soldiers, bringing the number of such incidents to four.
Each time information on these incidents has come from tips by reporters, anonymous phone calls or a letter from a soldier to his wife. Each time there has been a hurried-up investigation immediately afterward. Never have we had an honest, forthright, effective response from the Minister of National Defence.
When will this government acknowledge that the minister of defence is simply not fulfilling her responsibilities to her department or to the Canadian people? Will the Acting Prime Minister ensure there will be an open and complete account of these serious problems affecting our peacekeeping troops in Somalia and the reputation of Canada abroad?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the accusation that these incidents have not been reported simply is not true.
For example, the March 4 incident, which was the subject of some discussion here, the officers in charge on March 5, the day after, telephoned Canadian Press, Standard Broadcast News, CBC Newsworld and CBC Radio. It was widely reported in Canada.
Regarding the incident of March 16, a press release was issued in Mogadishu. It was not covered but there was no attempt to cover it up. The other two incidents were both reported in the media.

April 22, 1993
Oral Questions
In each situation an investigation was commenced. Two of the incidents were considered sufficiently serious that investigation teams were sent from DND to Somalia to investigate directly.
The minister of defence is in the legal system of DND and in fact has duties not dissimilar to those of a judge. Therefore she is limited in what she can say with respect to details of the cases.
I am sure the hon. member would appreciate that in the interests of justice, fairness and proper procedure in this matter, it would be most inappropriate for anyone in authority to give extensive details of the investigation.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. minister knows that in one case notice was given by posting a notice on the board. The other was simply a verbal account. In two cases there was no record of any press release being distributed.
In the CTV report last night the defence department admitted that investigations were under way in only two of the cases. It does not add up in anybody's estimation to a full, open and proper account. The consequences are serious. The defence chief of staff said in an interview in Maclean's'.
The Somali incidents may well be symptomatic of a breakdown of
our discipline and our leadership.
My serious question is this. Does the government, the Prime Minister and the Acting Prime Minister not think it is about time that we had a minister of defence in place who has the capacity, the interest and the time to deal with the serious problems affecting us in Somalia, to come to grips with the breakdown of discipline and leadership, in other words, to show there is some responsibility being shown at the top of the department of defence?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is wrong again in saying that only two of the incidents were investigated. That is not true. They were investigated. The investigations were initiated or started on site in all cases. In two of the cases it was found unnecessary to proceed further and in the other two cases it was found necessary to proceed further. That is exactly what is happening. That is what should properly happen in any circumstances.
The hon. member seems to have some doubts about the validity of the legal system within the Armed Forces and as a result of expressions of those doubts by himself and other members there have been some concerns raised. To allay those concerns the Judge Advocate General's department will be having a press availability session this afternoon to describe to all interested people exactly how the legal system works within the Armed Forces.
I am sure any fair-minded person will reach the conclusion that things are proceeding properly in a fair manner.

Mr. Speaker, it is not up to judges and lawyers to do so, but to the Minister of National Defence.
I must say how very concerned I am about the precarious situation of our troops in Bosnia and in Somalia. They are asked to disarm civilians, without having the mandate to protect these same people. According to Colonel Michael Dewar of the International Institute for Strategic Studies in London, Canadians do not have the necessary equipment to protect themselves.
Neither the Secretary of State for External Affairs nor the Minister of National Defence have reported these serious events to the House.
Will the government, the Prime Minister, ask that a complete report on the situation of our troops in Bosnia and in Somalia be tabled in the House? Will he see that we have a parliamentary debate on the peacekeeping role of Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not know how the hon. member has reached the conclusion that Canadian forces do not have the ability to protect themselves. They do indeed but perhaps not from the kind of innuendo the hon. member is putting forward in the House. speechtext:

Mr. Speaker, yes. Tomorrow we will debate Bill C-93, the government organizations act at third reading. This afternoon will be the first of eight allotted days during this supply period. Tomorrow will be the government organizations bill.
On Monday, prior to the budget address by the Minister of Finance at 4.30 p.m., there is a number of pieces of legislation we would like to deal with: Bill C-109, the bill dealing with privacy provisions for cellular phone use; Bill S-17, the intellectual property act; Bill C-72, the environmental round table act; Bill C-107, explosives act; and, Bill C-90, the sentencing act.

speechtext:

We oppose it for that reason and not for any other reason. For my friend to ask me to co-operate I have to say it is just not possible on this particular piece of legislation.
