speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: When the House rose the hon. member for Lambton-Middlesex had concluded his remarks. We will now proceed with the five-minute period of questions or comments.

Madam Speaker, this morning the hon. member for Lambton-Middlesex, who formerly was minister of
Agriculture under the Liberal government, made an extraordinary speech because he has a great heart and cares about his country, especially about agriculture in Canada.
I can tell you that I have often read his writings and they are always very informative on issues which are often complex. The hon. member for Lambton-Middlesex frequently tells us how, since 1984, the programs of the Conservative government have destroyed agriculture in Canada and have very often hurt producers and food processors.

I would greatly appreciate it if the hon. member for Lambton-Middlesex would give his thoughts and feelings on food production and processing in Canada, where it comes from and where it is going.

Madam Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague for the question.
First, I should reiterate the fact that Canadian food production and processing have the highest quality standards of any country in the world.
However I am growing increasingly alarmed at hearing the government say that we have to be more globally competitive. The government has not told us what that competition is.
I have a publication here called Viewpoint by Ernst and Young. It points out that in Europe the top 10 food manufacturers account for 60 per cent of the turnover among the top 40 companies.
We think this is a high level of concentration. In Canada the top five food distributors control 80 per cent and that is almost a monopolistic situation. In fact in some parts of the country one would have to term it that.
If we have to be globally competitive we cannot ignore the fact that there are some huge transnational corporations that control huge sectors of the U.S. agriculture industry in both production and processing.
One firm controls 25 per cent of chicken production and processing. Two firms control a huge volume of the beef processing. Between those two firms they slaughter
43,000	head of cattle a day. One of those firms has now bought a huge plant in Saltillo, Mexico.
April 22, 1993

How do we as Canadians compete against that type of thing? We do not have those volumes. On top of that, those huge firms have now been using a streamlined inspection system, or SIS, in terms of food quality. It simply means that it hires its own inspectors.
Last January a large number of children in Washington State became very ill. They were violently ill. In fact three of them died from food poisoning from eating contaminated hamburgers. Several more have permanent kidney damage. Some children in Abbotsford and Chilliwack had the same problems. I submit that this was a disaster waiting to happen. I talked about the quality standards prior to this in the House of Commons.
I maintain that our Canadian systems are the best in the world. We have to maintain those systems. We have to maintain the production systems across Canada that have been the best in the world and that have supplied Canadian consumers with high quality food at very reasonable prices. We can never afford, as Canadians, to let other corporations take control of our food supply.
As another member from eastern Ontario has pointed out on many occasions, food production and processing in Canada must be made a national security item.

Madam Speaker, I am particularly pleased to be able to stand up in this House today to debate what I consider an important motion, which is the devastating effects of this government's policies on jobs for Canadians.
While I recognize that there is a tremendous crushing and debilitating effect on those who have lost jobs directly, it goes beyond that. I want to talk about those spin-offs. Let us look at the situation to make sure that we are talking from the same sheet.
Since 1989, in the manufacturing sector alone, between 300,000 and 400,000 jobs have been lost. That is roughly 15 per cent. In the U.S. it has been 7 per cent. While the government argues about a world-wide recession, the U.S. has fared much better than Canada.
Let us look at some facts on the economy. The net public debt at the end of 1991-92 was $422.8 billion. That is much more than double the debt that the government
Supply
inherited in 1984. The federal deficit for 1991-92 was $34.6 billion. We see over the years that the deficit has exceeded $30 billion virtually all the time. The proposed deficit for 1992-93 was $34.4 billion. The deficit for the first 10 months of the fiscal year 1992-93 was $31.2 billion. The unemployment rate in March 1993 was 11 per cent. The number of Canadians unemployed was in excess of 1.5 million Canadians. The number of Canadians on welfare was in excess of 2.7 million. I have not talked about the food banks which will nourish well over two million Canadians this year.
Here are some other negative changes that have occurred. In 1988 there were 789,000 families experiencing unemployment. In 1992 it is 1.132 million. The unemployment rate in 1988 was 7.5 per cent. That is the average. In 1992 it was 11.5 per cent, which again is an average. What a deterioration. Youth unemployment is particularly close to my heart. In November 1988 it was 11.8 per cent. In February 1993 it was 16.7 per cent. The number of youths who have never worked was 350,000 on average in 1989. In 1991 it climbed to 412,000. In 1992 it was 475,000 and we expect it to be even higher in 1993.
Ask Canadians about their expectations for the future. We did ask this in 1988: Do you think the country and the economy will be stronger and will you be better off or worse off? In 1989, when we got the results, 28 per cent said that we would be better off. In 1992 it had gone down to 16 per cent. Those who said that we would be worse off were 41 per cent in 1989 and in 1992 it was 54 per cent.
I could give some more statistics but I think that I have made the point. The situation has deteriorated by virtually every single economic indicator that we use.
People will say: "You are a member of the opposition so obviously you are going to make statements like that". I want to draw the attention of the House to an article in The Gazette on April 16, 1993. The headline reads: "A national disaster, The real unemployment poll, A staggering 3.9 million people is a gaping wound in Canadian society, Catholic bishops say". What have been some of the headlines across the country? "Japanese owner shuts Trenton plant, Stamping plant to close in June, 91 to lose jobs".

April 22, 1993
Supply
In another article it says: "Auto plant closing to cost 200 jobs". In yet another one there is a map of southern Ontario and metro Toronto with all of the factories and commercial enterprises that have closed. There are many dots. "Job loss data points to manufacturing decline". It goes on to point out how serious it is.
Other articles say: "Where the jobs are disappearing, Job drain at critical mass to union: Hawker Siddeley taking Surrey plant south, Battered Cornwall loses 360 more jobs, 150 will lose jobs in a few months when Gatineau acoustic panel plant shuts, Penetang seat belt plant to move 194 jobs to Mexico, Aerospace plant closes, Auto parts plant closing: 115 jobs vanish". It goes on and on and on.
My province of Manitoba has not, in fact, been spared the devastation of the government's economic policies because it has on virtually every single indicator of poverty, the highest score in Canada. With youth poverty it is the worst record in Canada.
As I travel in my riding and as I travel through Winnipeg I see scores of plants and businesses that have closed and it looks like a devastated area.
As I indicated initially, it is extremely sad that those people have lost jobs because it impacts not only upon them but upon other members of the family and their immediate entourage in the community. It creates stress and a feeling of not being empowered to do anything about it.
There is something else that is often forgotten. Those job losses also assist other sectors. There is an important spin-off.
Let me give a number of critical examples from my riding, which is not unlike many others in Canada. In my riding there is the St. Boniface General Hospital, I'Hopi-tal General de St. Boniface. There are many, many job losses as a result of these closings, of this bankruptcy and of this economic situation that is not only recessionary but even worse. There is also those billions of dollars that have not been transferred over to the provinces.
I have in my own riding the College universitaire de St. Boniface that is the only French language university in western Canada. It too has been affected as have the other universities and the community colleges because of
the reduction in the transfer to provinces for education, training and retraining. It has been affected seriously. There are losses of jobs in those sectors. Community colleges are particularly hard hit. There are people lined up who cannot get the training that they require in order to dig themselves out of this hole called poverty.
There is simply not enough training. There are bankruptcies and closures everywhere. There are delays for new start ups. There are well-qualified and highly motivated people, sometimes with double degrees and sometimes journeymen and joumeywomen, who have excellent working records but cannot find jobs.
Let me give a few examples. There is a woman who is a new Canadian who had been a teacher and civil servant in her country. She is willing to take any job in order to help her family. She will have two daughters who will be going to university to be able to benefit from that which we have benefited in the past. Try as she might there is no work.
There is a person who because of health reasons needed to take early retirement but whose spouse developed difficult medical problems and needed some additional attention. He wants to supplement his income with a little extra work. He is well qualified and highly motivated. There is nothing there.
A married young man below the age of 30 is willing to undertake any job. There is nothing.
I could go on and on.

I believe I have nevertheless demonstrated that the policies of this government regarding job creation have failed and I would be pleased to answer any question from my government colleagues about my speeches or any other subject.

Madam Speaker, I listened to my hon. colleague from St. Boniface. I used to live in the suburb of Norwood in St. Boniface and I know of St. Boniface hospital.
I know from my friends still in Winnipeg that district in Manitoba has been very hard hit, as he has said. In fact I felt much closer to what he was saying because there are so many stories like that about southern Ontario. He has
April 22, 1993

made a very clear case that the present economy is not working and a change of course is needed.
On that basis I would like to ask the hon. member a two-part question. What does he feel will be the effect on the economy of southern Manitoba of the North American free trade agreement if it is adopted and brought into force? On the basis of whatever answer he gives to that first question, what is his party's intention regarding the North American free trade agreement?

Madam Speaker, I thank my hon. colleague for the question. How I wish he were still a resident of my riding of St. Boniface. In spite of his political preference I am sure he would probably support me during the next election.
I hope you would support me.

Of course I would. A gentleman like you, why would I not?
With respect to the very serious question of what my party's position is with respect to NAFTA, we have put it out time and time again. I feel very comfortable with that position. We have indicated that we cannot support NAFTA the way it is. We need a common set of trade rules. We need to ensure that environmental and labour standards are respected. We need to have security over energy and water.
Those are some of the issues that my leader has spoken about and that he is concerned about. He would make sure those were corrected and rectified before signing such an agreement. He has also said that this is a wonderful opportunity to correct the deficiencies of the Canada-U.S. trade agreement and I applaud him for having done that. By the way, he has also said that if we could not get those kinds of agreements we would abrogate.
There are those who would abrogate first but they would still have to negotiate. They have not proven their case that if they were to abrogate and then negotiate they would come up with a better package than we would if we were to sit down at the table and negotiate.
I feel very comfortable with our position. I think it is a responsible one. I am concerned as are many Canadians that if this is to go through the way it is, the kind of devastation I have described today will continue and it
Supply
must stop. It must absolutely stop. The country cannot take any more of it.

Madam Speaker, would not the hon. member have considered it useful if the bill had been defeated in the vote on second reading? Almost half of the members of the hon. member's caucus were absent for the vote. Those who were present voted against the bill on second reading but of course it was not enough to defeat second reading.
Can the hon. member comment on why almost half of his caucus chose to be absent so that while their votes of those present were recorded against it, the caucus as a whole allowed the second reading to go through by having nearly half the members absent and therefore not voting?

Madam Speaker, I know that I voted against it. I do not know whether it was half or almost half and I hesitate to speak for those who were absent. I think they can do that for themselves. I am sure there was no machiavellian plan, not that my colleague has suggested that, to try to help the government get it through. I assure the hon. member that is not true. They were solidly behind the leader and his policy. We do not want this bill to go through as it is. We need a standard code of trading rules. We need improved security with respect to labour and environmental standards and the points I have made. I assure my hon. colleague there is no hesitation on our part. Our position is clear. It is there. It will be followed and it will be respected.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Marc Robitaille (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, here we go again. Another simplistic motion condemning this government's economic policies. It is so easy for the opposition to produce motions without taking the time to really analyse the government's economic record. In fact, there is now a wave of optimism among Canadians about our economic recovery. And what do we get from members opposite? Another dose of pessimism and negative commentary. The usual unrelenting, repetitive and inaccurate criticism of the government's economic policies.

April 22, 1993
Supply
If my hon. colleagues do not know the facts, I will be glad to explain what those facts are. Only last week the Conference Board of Canada, an independent agency, predicted that economic growth will be even stronger than expected. Exports are up and inflation is very low. In fact we have the lowest inflation rate of any industrialized country. Interest rates are low and stable. The Canadian dollar is strong, and employment opportunities are improving. I know the unemployment rate is high. In any case one unemployed worker in this country will always be one too many. However, does the opposition realize that while the unemployment rate is high, there is optimism generated by our economic recovery among Canadians who are starting to look for work again?
Our government is willing to listen to constructive criticism that is documented and based on fact, not to negative criticism and unfounded accusations based on rumour.
Consider economic growth. Among the G-7 countries, Canada is outranked only by the United States on standard of living per capita, based on the gross domestic product. In recent years, strong economic growth has helped us close part of the gap that separates us from our prosperous neighbour to the south. Investment as a percentage of GDP is at its highest level in 25 years. On this point we outrank the United States and Germany. Manpower productivity is increasing while our production costs have gone down considerably. In addition substantial gains in productivity have enhanced Canada's competitive position on international markets.
The opposition referred to job losses, but do they realize that in the past few years, Canada created more jobs than any other G-7 country? Other countries envy our ability to create jobs. Although opposition members take the negative view, as usual, our government is committed to implementing positive policies that will guarantee sustainable growth.
And here is what we are already doing with that in mind: we are giving small businesses a 10 per cent tax credit for all machinery and equipment they will purchase this year. Furthermore, most businesses hiring new workers this year will not be subject to increases in
unemployment insurance premiums. I may remind the House that the opposition voted against these measures.
The government has extended the Small Business Financing Program for two years. This program allows companies to refinance loans at less than market rates.
We simplified the rules so as to encourage more investment in small business with RRSPs. We also raised the ceiling on loans under the Small Businesses Loans Act to $250,000.
Our government is not unaware that research and development is also essential to lasting economic growth. That is why we increased tax incentives for companies doing research and development by $230 million in the past five years. We have also set aside a $400 million reserve to overcome tax barriers to the technological development and the growth of business.
Our approach is as logical as can be. We ask Canadians to show self-discipline and to make short-term sacrifices so that our country can reap long-term benefits.
The only way to get rich quick is to win the lottery. Our government will not endanger Canadians' future economic well-being by unearthing the temporary one-shot job creation projects of the 1970s that went nowhere and cost them so dearly. We remember the old ideas of our Liberal friends. Like old ghosts from the past these Liberal candidates resurface, like the leader of the Liberal Party, a man of the past who, by the way, was a member of the House of Commons when John F. Kennedy was President of the United States. These people would take us back to the old recipes of bygone days, recipes which in the 1970s did not solve any problem, but indebted us, and we are still paying for them. They are just solutions from the past.
Our government has not continued on that dead-end path to put Canadians back to work. We want workers to attain a good standard of living and contribute to Canada's economic prosperity.
For this we have adopted a constructive approach that will produce lasting results in the long run. The opposition motions criticizing our government suggest that we should act as if our heavy debt burden did not exist. They are always trying to ignore it and asking us to act as
April 22, 1993

though there was no debt. All they want to do is spend and spend and spend. They love to spend other people's money.
That means living beyond our means and placing an undue financial burden in a completely irresponsible way on the shoulders of those who will come after us-our children and grandchildren. The government will not take that path. The Canadian people have given us the fundamental responsibility to act in the interest of the economy and we intend to live up to it.
Canada's greatest resource is its people and its workers. That is why our programs count on working people. They show the confidence we have in their initiative, our confidence in the imagination, determination and dynamism of the workers of this country.
As the amendments we made to the unemployment insurance plan show, we are convinced that Canadian workers can succeed. We can no longer spare those who do not act responsibly enough to keep their jobs, simply because they do not want to work. We appeal to their deep sense of self-esteem and we ask them to contribute to the economic recovery.
We must emphasize training. We absolutely must prepare Canadian workers so that they can take their place in the world economy which is moving ahead rapidly and is based on knowledge and high technology. Every day, workers tell our employment counsellors that they want training. Training is almost everybody's top priority. They do not want to be subsidized by collecting unemployment insurance. They want to have a reasonable chance to get better jobs. They want training.
To meet this demand during the fiscal year which just ended, we spent $3.5 billion to enable 685,300 Canadian workers to participate in government programs relating to the labour market.
During this new fiscal year, we will spend about $3.8 billion on programs and services related to the labour market. I think that even my hon. colleagues will agree that this is a significant increase, compared to the $2.1 billion spent in 1985-86. Of the $3.8 billion, $2.21 billion will be spent on specific training and adjustment initiatives for UI claimants in the context of the so-called developmental uses. This amount is the largest ever spent on developmental uses in the UI account. It is 13 per cent more than last year and almost four and one
Supply
half times more than the $500 million budgeted in 1990. What is so terrible is the fact that the opposition voted against these excellent initiatives.
We are talking not only about expenditures but also about investment. I wonder if my hon. colleagues understand that. The economic downturn is an integral part of global restructuring; it is useless to attempt to put the blame on the government and its actions. If my colleagues from the opposition displayed a little bit of intellectual honesty, they would clearly tell the population that a large part of our present problems are due to a restructuring of the world economy.
The government is not sitting idle, waiting to see what will happen. In spite of all the negative and senseless objections made by the opposition, we take positive measures to help workers face the competition more easily once the economic recovery is definitely under way.
This year one million UI claimants should get some occupational training while receiving benefits. This is how we invest these $2.1 billion. I challenge my hon. colleagues to propose a better way to invest in Canada's future.
Occupational training is certainly the top priority for workers who have had many productive years and who suddenly find themselves unemployed because of this industrial restructuring at the international level. This is the reality and when we talk to workers, they recognize that reality.
Workers who have been laid off and who have worked uninterruptedly for at least five consecutive years have a well established work ethic. They know what they want. They want training and professional development in order to rejoin the labour force. And the government fully intends to provide them with this training.
Our government will spend $300 million to help put these people back to work as soon as possible. To this end we will create partnerships with business communities and organizations. We are in the process of setting up local adjustment committees to meet the particular needs of the clientele. These initiatives are taken to improve our economy.
I also wonder if my hon. colleagues know that our work sharing program enables us to use the UI fund so as to avoid lay-offs. In periods of work slowdowns, employers can keep workers who agree to work a shorter week and who are eligible for UI benefits for the down days.

April 22, 1993
Supply
These are among the other initiatives taken by our government.
Experience has taught us that the government must allow the private sector to have direct input regarding the use of federal resources to solve problems related to the labour market. These employers are important stakeholders. We have also learned that the private sector must spend more time, make more efforts and use more resources, so that we have skilled workers who are able to face the competition.
The government helps to achieve these objectives by gathering together business people and other stakeholders in powerful and effective sector groups.
Working together with the business community and other stakeholders, we have already set up 17 sectoral councils to help promote continuing training. But that is a fact that the opposition forgets to mention, does not remember and fails to recognize. We are now improving this positive approach through a five-year plan, the sectoral partnerships initiative in which we are investing $352 million. This program, which has recently received an extra $250 million in funding, will enable Canadian business to face the human resources challenges confronting it and to do so within the scope of the program. It is essential, for one thing, to establish clearly what skills workers will need to enable Canada to remain competitive in the future. This is a major aspect of our strategy that the opposition has deliberately omitted.
With this in view, the number of sectorial councils will be increased by 38, to a total of 55. These councils will look into human resource development, a challenge now facing Canadian business. The sectoral partnerships initiative is based on the premise that the private sector is responsible for training workers on the job. However, we lag far behind our global competitors when it comes to manpower development. That is why our government will once again act responsibly and provide leadership on this issue.
Under this new program, tax incentives for training programs in industry can be created and even more workers can be trained under cost-sharing agreements signed with the government's partners. The sectoral
councils will also develop new and improved occupational standards to increase performance and job opportunities for 3.5 million Canadian workers.
I would like to point out that the new program will not be implemented at the expense of short-term job creation programs as the government intends it as a long-term job creation plan. However, our immediate concern should be, and is indeed, putting Canadians back to work.

The previous speaker may criticize the opposition but the facts are there and opposition members are not alone in condemning the government for its economic policies. Last week the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops asked the government to act. The bishops begged the Conservative government to do something about the high unemployment rate in this country. They said that the economic policies of the past decade had put an undue burden on the workers in this country.
According to the bishops, Canada is experiencing a social crisis that is unprecendented, with one-quarter of its labour force shut out of the labour market. If the government finds it hard to believe opposition members or Canada's bishops, let us take a look at the figures published by the government's own agency, Statistics Canada.
If it compares today's figures with 1988, the government will see the economic situation in this country has worsened. In 1988 there were 789,000 Canadian families with one member unemployed. In 1992 there were 1,132,000, an increase of over 43 per cent. In 1988 the unemployment rate was 7.5 per cent. In 1992 it was 11.5 per cent. Today more than 1.5 million Canadians are unemployed. In November 1988 the youth unemployment rate in this country was 11.8 per cent. Today it is up to 16.7 per cent.
The situation is just as depressing in Quebec's main urban centres. Between March 1992 and March 1993, the unemployment rate went up in Chicoutimi, Jonquiere, Trois-Rivieres and Montreal, where more than 225,000 people get unemployment insurance benefits.
Consider the number of jobs lost since January 1989 in the manufacturing sector. Canada has lost 319,000 jobs in this sector. The hon. member told us that exports had gone up. That is all very well, but according to Statistics Canada, since 1989 we lost 319,000 jobs in the manufac-
April 22, 1993

turing sector, a sector that is vital to our economy. This means 15 per cent of all the jobs in this sector.
In Quebec 115,000 jobs were lost in the manufacturing sector during the same period. This represents a loss of 19 per cent in a sector that is extremely important to the economy of Quebec and the Montreal region. Meanwhile, in the United States only 7 per cent of the jobs in this sector disappeared.
These are Statistics Canada figures, not mine. The hon. member said earlier that we had just come out of a recession that was caused by the international economic situation. Job losses and high unemployment rates result in pauperizing the population. Montreal is a case in point. Last week one of the headlines read "Montreal: Poverty Capital". That is where we are after nine years.

This change has been brought to this world of production and distribution by computerization, by satellites, by the transmission of data, equipment and knowledge, by robotization in plants and equipment in factories and so on. These things so dramatically change the way we do things that they have distorted and upset the entire production system of the world.

We have a sound money policy. We have beaten down inflation to its lowest rate in 30 years. Prices do not rise unrealistically any more. Our inflation rate in Canada is
April 22, 1993

the lowest of the OECD countries. That took some doing. That put some blood on the floor. However our inflation rate is down so that our money is sound money.
Why do people buy our bonds? Not because they like the looks of us. They buy them because our money is sound money. It will buy today and tomorrow the same amount of goods and services, and that is the kind of thing people want when they lend money to a country or invest in a country. A sound money policy is essential for Canada.
We have developed a fair tax policy. We have done everything conceivable in the last eight and a half years to change the Income Tkx Act to get away from all the hidden little wrinkles that were in it to let the rich make more, to let the fast operators make more. We have done that deliberately, capably, and competently. Our Income Tax Act is probably fairer today than at any time in our history.
I am not saying that taxes are ever fair. Taxes are never fair to the beholder. Somebody looks at someone else and says: "They have more than I have. Perhaps they should pay more tax than I should". Our tax system today is fairer than ever before.
A corporate tax system has to be not just fair but competitive. My friends in the New Democratic Party would like to put greater burdens on the corporate tax system. They forget that we are in a world of competition, that companies earn their profits where they pay the least amount of tax. If we make our taxes higher than in countries that are our trading partners then, guess what? The profit will not be made here. It will be made somewhere else and transfer pricing provides no possibility of ever following it through. We could never with all the accountants in the country follow through all of the possibilities of transfer pricing.
In the last budget we made our corporate tax for manufacturers on average 2 per cent less than the manufacturing corporate tax rate in the United States. That is a very substantial advantage to those who would set up plants and businesses in Canada.
We have in this country, and have had for a long time, a sales tax system. Lots of people object to sales taxes, to commodity taxes. Before this Parliament began we had a sales tax system which put a 13.5 per cent tax on people
Supply
who manufactured in the country. That tax gave an advantage to foreigners who brought goods into the country because they only paid tax at their plant gate and the cost of bringing goods here was not included in their tax base. Therefore we changed that commodity tax system to the goods and services tax.
That tax may have some problems with it. It may need some ironing out. It may need some work and massaging. A bill was passed by this House just recently to do that. Bit by bit we will have that tax system working very smoothly.
However that tax system is the fairest form of commodity tax system that the world knows. Indeed, 45 other countries in the world have that tax system.
To say that this is the wrong system, that a VAT tax system is not a good system, is to say that everybody else in the world is stupid and we know better than they do. That is the attitude of the New Democrats and the Liberals because they have not thought it through. They criticize us but they do not think it through.
In this great world of change we also must make sure that we try to train and retrain people for jobs, that we give people adjustment programs. This year we are spending $4 billion on retraining and training people on a national basis. That is infinitely more than was ever spent before, massively more. We have changed the system to try to train and retrain people, to try to get people to adapt to new circumstances, to new job opportunities, to new careers. We are all going to have to adapt to new ways of doing things.
In government we have adapted to new ways of doing things. Changes have taken place in employment and immigration in terms of how one files an immigration form. Those ways are very much changed. They are very much changed to take advantage of the systems that are now available. They are very much changed in the way the post office operates to deliver mail. These are changes that must take place. These changes will continue to take place. They must continue to take place.
We have to be internationally competitive. We cannot continue to do things in the old way because the old way is not good enough. The old way will give us a very poor standard of living. Our standard of living will drop and

April 22, 1993
Supply
drop if we continue with the old ways. We cannot carry on with old ways in a world of change.
We have done a great deal to promote science and technology. In a world of change we have to be brighter and we have to be ahead of other people. From 1984 to 1993 we have increased by 44 per cent direct government spending on science and technology, in grants and so on. Today we spend $200 million a year just on small businesses to allow them special credits in terms of their science and technology development. We have developed a series of centres of excellence across Canada in which we try to bring in scientists and engineers to work on new and important manufacturing and technological development.
Just recently in this House we passed Bill C-91 which gave further patent protection on intellectual property. That bill has been criticized but I have recently attended two major plant openings with major investment in my city of Mississauga. Yesterday Astra Pharma opened a facility and announced another $200 million in further investment in plant, laboratories, and assistance to people in universities to develop new pharmaceutical products. That company is manufacturing painkilling products today for export to the world. It has a world mandate.
With the huge investments in this kind of work, these are not small companies. These are companies that produce high quality jobs for people with doctorate or masters degrees. These are people we need to create a better society. This is not about flipping hamburgers. This is about building Canada. This is about building a better future for all of us. It is a question of the science and technology work we have been doing.
We have a special program for students. The scholarship arrangement qualifies 3,300 young people in our high schools across Canada every year for scholarships at universities. These scholarships are for $3,000 for a four year course at university in science and technology. The students have to be bright to get them but there are 3,300. That is a lot of assistance to young people who are going to help build our nation.
We recognize that if we are going to have jobs we have to assist small business. This House just recently passed a very major change to the Small Businesses Loans Act,
increasing the limit of that loan to $250,000, making it possible for the money in the loan to indirectly be worked into working capital credit because it does not require a 100 per cent guarantee. It does not require that the proprietor put his house on the line, his blood on the line. He only has to guarantee 25 per cent of the loan.
Tell me where you can get a bank loan and only sign for 25 per cent of the capital. They only have to guarantee 25 per cent of it. Banks have come forward and said they are going to put that money up but not at 1.75 per cent over prime as they are entitled to under the act. The Bank of Nova Scotia has come forward and said it likes the statute so much it is going to lend the money at prime. The Bank of Montreal is matching it.
Members talk about not doing things but that is pretty important work. We have a 10 per cent tax credit for small business if they buy manufacturing equipment. That comes right off their tax. In effect, with a tax credit of 10 per cent and a small business tax rate of 12 per cent, small businessmen pay precious little corporate tax if they spend their profits in buying equipment. That is assistance that makes our small businesses work effectively.
In order to encourage businesses to hire people a UI holiday was provided for small businesses that pay less than $30,000 a year in UI premiums. A small business with five, six or ten employees which does not have to pay $30,000 in UI can hire people and not make any UI contribution for this year.
That is after you have raised the rate 35 per cent.
My friend says we have raised the rate. We did not raise the rate. We reduced the benefit a bit but we did not raise the rate.
You raised the rates twice in one year.
We kept the rates where they had been and they would have gone up if we followed the bill the way you wanted us to do.
Get the facts.

They want us to ensure the country does not work the way it can work best. This Parliament has had one situation after another where the opposition has ganged up to try to prevent things happening to make the country work better.
April 22, 1993

We have been working very diligently to trim government costs. We have privatized 23 Crown corporations, wound up 14 Crown corporations, wound up and consolidated 40 agencies and activities of the government in boards and other things. Most important, we have pushed and pushed to blast our way to the markets of the world. With the free trade agreement, our sales to the United States last year were $122.3 billion. That left us a very substantial surplus with that country.
More important, we are currently entering into agreements under the North American free trade agreement to tie in Mexico. We are exploring agreements to tie in Chile and Argentina. Right now the Minister for International Trade is on his way to Argentina again to explore more deals and more potential trade. By the way, he has taken the critic for the Liberal Party with him. Maybe together they can get the trade deal organized.
If we are going to be successful, this country that is expert at a limited number of things has to sell that expertise where it can. We have to be able to sell it everywhere in the world. We can and we will.
Last, may I point to the fact that our financial industries have been revamped so that our banks, trust companies and insurance companies will even more be able to compete in the international financial world.
In the Bahamas.
Cayman Islands. Do they pay?

We think of services as not being profitable. At least one-third of the business of Canadian banks is in foreign markets making money for Canada and bringing back the head office jobs that keep young people employed, give us opportunities and make jobs. Fifty-five per cent of the activity of Canadian life insurance companies is in foreign markets. The head office work for those companies, the policy designed for those companies, is done in Canada and employs Canadians.
We are criticized by people who say we have not done anything. We are in a world of rough change. We have competed better than anyone else in this world of change. Our growth rates are awful but compared to our colleagues in other countries they are superb.
Supply
We brought down the deficit as a percentage of the economy. Our interest rates are down very dramatically again, another 10 basis points this week. Our tax system is fair and more competitive. Our trade agreements give us key access to new export markets. Our labour productivity is growing strongly. We are on the verge of a new beginning. I am proud to say this government has done its best to cope with change.

Madam Speaker, I listened to my hon. friend from Mississauga and while I like him personally, I do not agree with anything he says. I want to make a short statement and I have a question for him.
The other day somebody was describing the government's approach to the economy. He said: "When a family finds itself in a serious debt situation because of accumulated debts the way to respond to that debt is not to resign from your employment and go on UIC". Somehow I think that symbolizes the approach of this government. It feels that by putting more people out of work by causing more small businesses to go bankrupt, somehow this is going to help the economy. This is a puzzling approach. Nevertheless it is where my friend and I disagree.
My question is this. The other day a young woman from Kamloops who is in grade 10 asked me this question. She is a very serious young student and has studied the free trade agreement. Kate Thrley is her name.

April 22, 1993
Supply
She told me she did not understand why the government was going ahead with the NAFTA legislation. I replied that I did not either. She said: "Imagine, Mr. Riis, if you won $10 million in the lottery today. You want to start a new factory or plant and are going to invest your money with the idea of making a profit in the years ahead. You have four choices. You can pay your employees $18 an hour as we do in some of our manufacturing plants in Canada. You can go to the northern part of the United States to the rust belt area and pay $12 an hour for the same level of expertise. You can go to Louisiana, Alabama, Tennessee and west Texas and pay $6.50 for the same level of expertise. Now, under NAFTA, you can go to Mexico and pay 60 cents an hour for that same expertise".
It is five cents in the Dominican Republic.

Or five cents an hour in the Dominican Republic as my friend indicates. This of course is the next extension of the NAFTA agreement.
The student said: "Mr. Riis, unless you are crazy, if you are interested in maximizing your profits and have a choice of paying $18 an hour, $12 an hour, $6 an hour or 60 cents an hour where would you locate your plant?"
I responded that it seemed obvious to me that I would be encouraged to locate it in Mexico. Of course that is the motivation behind at least 2,000 corporate decisions to move and open plants in the Maquiladora zone in northern Mexico and employ 500,000 people there. Salaries average about 60 cents an hour.
As Ross Perot said, as soon as the North American free trade agreement is signed by Mexico, the United States and Canada, we are going to hear this massive flushing sound as the jobs are flushed from Canada and the United States into Mexico. This young woman called Kate Tbrley said that she believed in Ross Perot's view of the issue.
I want to ask my hon. friend from Mississauga this. If he was going to open that plant and he had the choice of paying employees in Canada $18 an hour or paying employees with the same level of expertise and training 60 cents an hour in Maquiladora zones in northern Mexico, where would he locate his plant being the entrepreneurial person that he is?

Madam Speaker, I want to give my friend a little lesson.
I was at the opening of a further extension of a plant by Astra pharmaceuticals in my riding yesterday. I had a chat with the CEO of that company whose head office is in Sweden.
It also has an office in Mexico. The company puts pills together in Mexico but it does not make any chemicals there because it cannot find any trained labour. It cannot find the equipment.
It has to put the stuff for the pills into a pill making machine that pumps the pills out in Mexico. All the stuff that makes the pills possible is manufactured in Canada or Sweden. It is not manufactured in Mexico and probably never will be.
Fie said: "What we are is a highly competent technical business. Therefore we have to have the best expertise possible. There is no way that you could possibly operate our business in a place where you did not have a level of competence that would make it possible".
I want to say to my friend, if you have a job that can be done by any jerk who has no education and pay him $18 an hour in this competitive world then you have a problem. If you have a job that must be done by someone who has confidence, who can understand a computer and run robotics, who can handle things effectively and efficiently you had better hire the best highly trained labour you possibly can.
Labour is not the cost in these things. In good, well-organized plants, labour represents about 10 per cent of the cost at the most. You can get your labour for 50 cents a day in south China or Bangladesh. Mexico is expensive. It costs about $2.33 an hour. Mexico is a high labour place in comparison to the Bangladeshes of this world, if one wants really cheap labour then one goes to a place where one can get really cheap labour. However, Mexico is not that kind of place. Mexico is a place where labour costs are expensive if one has to have any degree of technical capacity. The other facilities that go along are continuously more expensive.
We have a company in my constituency called Sissons that currently is in the business of building auto parts.
April 22, 1993
At $2 an hour?

I want to tell Nelson this. We have a policy in this government with the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development where he will sponsor someone to open a plant in an Indian reserve and he will actually pay all the labour costs. It will not cost you a nickel. However, I do not see people flooding Indian reserves to open plants.
The reason is this. One must open a plant where one has competent people and competent equipment and competent facilities. One may get all worked up about some poor Mexican who needs a job-he probably does-but remember that the jobs we have to have in this country are jobs that are not untrained jobs. They are jobs for people who are competent and capable. We have to build a market for our competent and capable and highly expert material.
Are you saying Mexicans are not competent? Where have you been in Mexico, Tijuana? They have universities in Mexico.

one moment say that the way the GST is presently operating and running is nearly as smooth or effective or competent as it should be. That is going to take some time for our people in the Department of National

Revenue to organize. There is no question about it. A tax system that taxes every trade transaction in the whole production system requires more people to follow it up than a tax system that taxes only once at the manufacturer's level. However, the fact is that that type of tax system is fairer and more organized to the benefit of the country than any other system. Madam Speaker, I am pleased to rise today to participate in this debate on a motion put forward by my colleague:
That this House condemn the government for policies which have decimated the economy forcing company closures resulting in job losses for Canadian workers.
I want to talk about the experience of northwestern Ontario over the last number of years where we have seen community after community decimated by the economic realities in part caused by the federal government.
Let me first start with the community of Atikokan which is a remarkable community in my riding that in 1979-80 saw 1,100 highly paid mining jobs disappear when the two iron ore mines closed.
Following that closure, the community struggled. Prior to the closure, the community worked with an adjustment committee to begin the process of looking for new opportunities. Some were forthcoming and some came and went.
We got to the point a little over two years ago where the community had rebounded. We had two wood-based companies. Proboard Ltd. was a manufacturer of a type of particle board panelling. There was also the Atikokan Forest Products Division at Sapawe down the road about 30 miles. It was a sawmill.
One will remember that around that time the policy of the federal government was to impose a 15 per cent tax on Canadian exporters of softwood lumber. At the same time our dollar was high in relation to the American dollar. Let us remember that the vast majority of our trade always has been and probably always will be with our neighbour to the south. Irrespective of the free trade agreement or the North American free trade agreement,

April 22, 1993
Supply
that is where the big market is and that is where we need to go to sell a lot of our goods and services.
Two years and a couple of months ago the unemployment rate in the community of Atikokan was 80 per cent. Why? Because of softwood lumber, high interest rates and the high dollar. Both mills were shut down.
The community pulled together. Management, unions, the municipality, the school board, the social service agencies and everybody got together along with their provincial and federal members of Parliament.
Howard Hampton, the provincial member for the Rainy River riding, then the Attorney General for the province of Ontario and a New Democrat, went to bat provincially. I, on the other hand, got in touch with senior ministers in the Conservative cabinet here in Ottawa who have responsibility for economic matters, employment matters or what have you.
I can say very accurately that the only help that the people of Atikokan got was from the NDP government of Ontario. Those two mills exist today because of the assistance they were given. It was not any giveaway or corporate welfare but innovative financial help that allowed those two facilities to exist today.
One of them still has a rocky road ahead of it. It is up and down in terms of the operation but it is still there. Atikokan Forest Products Division is expanding because of the turnaround in softwood lumber since the 15 per cent tax was dropped.
One of the key elements in both those situations was that the unions and the companies and the Ontario government worked in partnership to develop a plan of action. That would not have happened under a Liberal or a Conservative government in Ontario.
Let me go to the other end of my riding that is the community of Thunder Bay itself. Actually parts of it are in Thunder Bay and outside my riding. We have another situation where one pulp and paper mill shut its doors and the process of stripping the equipment was begun. That is Abitibi's Thunder Bay mill. We had a second mill in crisis. The community was in danger of losing yet another mill.
I want to talk about the workers in Thunder Bay who made some tough decisions. Perhaps if the Liberals would listen to me as opposed to wondering about the members in the House we might be able to get on with things.
The situation that exists in Thunder Bay at the paper mill was that Abitibi basically said: "We cannot afford to keep this mill any more. We are going to sell this mill and if we do not get a buyer we are going to close it". This is again a case where a community pulled together. The employees of the mill, both the management employees and the various unions that represent the workers, got together with the province of Ontario.
Through long, hard bargaining they first worked out an agreement between the management employees and the union employees to decide: "Yes, we want to buy the mill. We the people of the community and we the workers want to buy that mill". Whether it was management workers or union workers, they wanted to buy the mill. The province of Ontario came with them and said that it would assist them. It said: "We will provide you with a combination of loans and loan guarantees to allow you to take this step".
It was not easy for the workers. They knew that even if they did this some of their colleagues would not be there working beside them because they would have to reduce the numbers. As a community we lost because of that. They also recognized that they would have to compress their wages and in fact take some cuts but they were prepared to live with that.
However, this is again an example of where groups worked together: the workers, both management and union; the unions; the province; and Abitibi-Price which agreed to sell the mill to the employees. This mill is the first ever, 100 per cent employee owned pulp and paper mill in Canada. Any of the other mills are a combination of employee ownership with somebody else. It is a success story in the sense that they work together.
There are three similarities to these two projects. First, it would have been impossible without the province of Ontario and the assistance that it provided these groups. Second, it would have been impossible without the co-operation of all the players. Third, in neither of
April 22, 1993

these projects did the federal government lift one finger to assist these plants in northwestern Ontario to survive.
We tried employment and immigration and FEDNOR. They wrote nice letters long after the fact but that is all they did in response to the needs of the community.
The crisis is not over. Just a couple of weeks ago Canadian Pacific Forest Products announced that it was shutting down one of its kraft mills in Thunder Bay. Up our way it is not like GM closing a particular plant when we talk about plant closures. This is because in a large number of cases it carves off a chunk of the mill. It is really two, three or four mills in one. It closes one of those mills but the other ones keep operating. It is not the same as a whole factory having the doors locked.
It is another 350 jobs. That actually brings it up to, in terms of the number of jobs lost in and around the community of Thunder Bay in the pulp and paper sector alone, about 1,500 or 1,600 in the last two years. On top of that, the grain industry and the transportation industry have been decimated because of the shift of grain to the west coast. We used to handle 60 to 70 per cent of the export grain. We are now down to around 30 per cent.
Can-Car, which in a year or so will be doing great thanks to the Government of Ontario for ensuring that the TTC allocated its contracts to an Ontario plant rather than letting them go offshore, will have between 800 and 1,000 people working there for the next 10 years.
It is crisis after crisis and the federal government has done nothing to effect a positive change in northwestern Ontario. Even though for years it has recognized the inequities in the Western Grain Transportation Act it has refused to eliminate the distortions that make it cheaper to send grain to the west coast. We would rather leave it to the marketplace. Let the market decide which way the grain should go. We would be quite prepared to accept that. The federal government has done nothing to assist the people of Thunder Bay and northwestern Ontario.
I think it is appropriate to quote from an opinion piece called "Viewpoint" which appeared in the Thunder Bay Chronicle-JournallTimes-News on Saturday, April 17. This is another part of the element and it fits into the debate we have been having about the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement and the North American free trade
Supply
agreement between Canada, U.S., and Mexico in terms of decision making. For years most of our employment in northwestern Ontario was locally owned. In fact, Abitibi Provincial is now coming back under local ownership because the employees decided to buy it, but the rest of our major employers are controlled elsewhere.
The grain companies are based in western Canada, those that are part of the pools, or in the case of Cargill elsewhere in the world. Can-Car is owned by Bombardier based out of Montreal.
Soon to go to Mexico.

Hopefully it is not going to Mexico. It cannot seem to get contracts in Mexico even though it has a plant there. The control is elsewhere. Abitibi is controlled out of another part of Canada. Canadian Pacific Forest Products is also controlled out of Montreal. It does not matter where it is, it is the fact that the control is not local.
Let me read the article written by Robert Zobatar who is a forest industry worker. It is entitled "A blue collar insider's view of wood woes. Companies are placing undue blame on unions". He says:
For the past 23 years I have earned my living in the pulp and paper industry. I have worked at Abitibi's pulp mills and the woodlands operations of Abitibi, Canadian Pacific Forest Products (CPFP) and Buchanan Forest Products. I have met and gotten to know hundreds of workers, some unionized and some not, young people and old people. I have experienced first hand the attitudes and work ethic of these people from days gone by to the present. I can safely say that the workers and the unions are not the unyielding, radical, unwashed masses that big companies such as CPFP try to make us out to be.
In their most recent press releases, CPFP suggests that next to economic and market conditions, the closure of the softwood pulp mill is the result of the union's unwillingness to accept proposals for modified work practices. Poppycock. In the real world, you don't receive something for nothing. CPFP may be selling softwood pulp for less than it costs to produce it, and suffering a loss, but the fact remains they are not giving it away for free. They are still receiving something for their product. By the same token, unions and workers are not about to give away concessions and receive nothing in return, i.e. job security.
Behind the scenes, officials of these big companies suggest to the workers that we can't see the big picture, we don't understand things, and we are ruining the companies. Well, most of us stayed in school long enough to learn to read. We are quite aware of the ever-expanding global economy, the world economic crunch, the information era, and the need for change. We are also very much aware of such things as corporate raiding, buy-outs, cover-ups, profit margins, bottom lines, and shareholders-in general greed. If workers really are narrow-minded, then companies such as CPFP are doubly so. They can't see past profit and loss and shareholders. When the more community-involved Great Lakes Forest Products sold out to

April 22, 1993
Supply
CPFP, such things as the human factor and community spirit began diminishing and are now on the verge of extinction.
Economic conditions aside, why is the company in such dire straits anyhow? They were equal partners in negotiating the existing union contracts, and didn't sign those contracts thinking they couldn't afford them. Could there have been some poor management decisions, a lack of foresight on mechanization, poorly done studies on some of the new technology they so heavily invested in? Heaven forbid, they should admit to such mistakes.
I have seen this company spend many millions of dollars on every new piece of forestry equipment that came along (machines that can cost a $ 1 /4 million or more) only to discover a few years later that it is obsolete, doesn't perform to expectations, or destroys the regenerative environment.
I have seen many seasoned bush workers offer advice on how to try and make something work, only to be shunned by a young pup foreman fresh out of forestry school whose only concern was to assert his authority over the worker.
When CPFP sold their stud lumber mill last year, I watched as almost to the day that the last piece of equipment was being removed from that mill, Hurricane Andrew struck in the U.S., and the price of lumber skyrocketed. Who did they sell that equipment to? Their arch rival, Buchanan Forest Products, who are now making windfall profits with it.
What did they do with the proceeds of the sale of equipment from the wafer board plant and the stud mill? They received large amounts of grant money to build those plants and also modernize the Dryden and Thunder Bay pulp mills as well. Remember all those headlines in the 70s when things were going well? Have we ever seen headlines about returning money to the government when they sell this equipment, or about helping laid-off workers? No! I suspect that such money will be squandered on the next bit of flash in the pan technology that comes along.
I can only hope that while this company is looking so closely at what the unions can do for it, it is also looking closely at what it can do for itself. I know that with the impending expiration of mill and woodlands contracts, the unions, in view of recent events, are seriously considering the way of the future. Time will tell what comes of it all. Perhaps if we had all paid more heed to Alvin Toffler in 1975 when he published his book The Third Wave, we would have been better prepared for the mess we are all in today.
There is no question that the economy in northwestern Ontario is hurting. It is not just the visible mill jobs. It is not just the visible jobs in the elevators. It is not just the visible jobs at Port Arthur shipyard, which is being drastically downsized as a result of the policies of the federal government to get us out of the shipbuilding and ship repair industry as a nation. There are also hundreds
of spin-off jobs that existed because of those main jobs being in place.
There are also smaller companies that are not as visible, that are off the main track, that have gone away, that will not come back, and that cannot come back because the product they produced is now being produced much cheaper elsewhere, whether in the southern United States or in Mexico even today let alone when the North American free trade agreement comes into effect.
We have to do better than just look after those workers who have lost their jobs by providing them with training. I recognize that there will be restructuring. A society that does not change is a dead society, no question about that. It is how we do it. It is what things we put in place to protect the people, to protect the industries where necessary. We have to keep in mind that these are all people, they have families, they have children, they contribute to the community, they are members of our church or our service club, they are everybody and we all have a responsibility.
We cannot just leave things to the marketplace to decide. There needs to be a role for governments to ensure the orderly progression of whatever restructuring is necessary in society.
I appreciate this opportunity to participate in this debate today. I just wish the government were really listening.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the remarks of the member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan. This is clearly a world of change and he will realize that when he travels, if he does, to the southern United States. Where they used to have cotton fields they now have forests of pine that grow to pulpwood size in less than 25 years and are harvested by automatic machinery so that the lumber or wood is never touched by human hands. Of course we in northern Ontario have the same type of machinery but we do not have quite the same easy access to the wood supply that technology has given them. Our paper, while it is first class, is in very tough competition with other paper sources in the world and other wood products in the world.
April 22, 1993

I was wondering if in the restructuring of companies in his area whether he has a place that takes advantage of the changes we have made in the Income Tax Act that enable people to invest up to 10 per cent in the ownership of a company by using their private RRSPs. That means that they can in effect invest in their own company without paying income tax on the investment. In his area had he been promoting that rather beneficial arrangement for the assistance of people in developing small businesses and small business ownership and family business and for making capital available for people to build their own job opportunities?

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the member for Mississauga South for his question.
I will respond in two ways. I would be very nervous about encouraging anybody to put at risk money which is designed to ensure that they have an appropriate income at the time they reach their retirement age. By diverting even a part of their RRSPs in a venture is not something I would go out and campaign for. It is obviously something that each individual would have to look at in terms of their own financial circumstances.
I can say we are very frustrated about the work being done by my colleague, the member for Sault Ste. Marie, in trying to convince the federal government to match what Ontario has done. This was in terms of allowing individuals who purchased shares of their companies to consider them as tax deductions. It is much like what was tried for Algoma Steel. My understanding is that it cannot be done and the government has refused to bring that forward.
Here is the other point. I discovered this after a colleague of mine was given notice that the job he had for 17 years is gone. He works in one of the grain related industries. The dilemma he now faces is he knows he is going to get severance pay and quite a decent package. He also knows that under the UI Act passed by this Parliament and moved by the Conservatives that that severance pay will be treated as earnings for a prescribed period of time. He had wanted to take that money and invest it in a small business that would provide him with employment. He is in his 50s. We all know the reality of workers at that age. They are not as employable as workers at age 45, 30 or 25 because of the length of time
Supply
the employers see they will get back from their investment. He recognizes that but he is caught between a rock and a hard place.
He knows that if he takes that $20,000 and puts it into a small business he will have no income because he will be ineligible for unemployment insurance because the assumption is that the money will be used to replace unemployment insurance for up to 52 weeks. It is a real dilemma and it has been created by this government. Even though I know that was not the intention, it has actually worked against what the member has been suggesting, which is getting more people to invest in small business in those kinds of ways.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened to the hon. member's speech. I wish the hon. member for Mississauga South had been a little more pointed in his question. I will try to make the point perhaps a little clearer.

I think he must recognize the gravity of that problem. I am sure he also recognizes that these jobs are not coming back. As he knows, Ontario is saddled with an NDP government which is driving investment out of the province.
We know that the economies in British Columbia-
They are driving us crazy.

I was not going to go that far. He knows that jobs are being created in British Columbia and Alberta at the present time because those governments are much more enlightened. One of them is an NDP government I admit. It is more enlightened than the Ontario government, which seems to be unusually doctrinaire in its approach to social problems in our province.
I know he is a friend of the premier. There is a colleague of the premier in this House. I have suggested that the premier receive tutelage at the knees of some of the hon. members here. I would not want to suggest that the hon. member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan had been here long enough to tutor the premier of Ontario.

April 22, 1993

I wonder if he would agree with me that the appropriate advice for the premier is to get out of office. He is driving investment out of Ontario. He is stopping job creation in Ontario. In fact, if we had any other government in Ontario today, Ontario would be out of the recession.

If that is so, would he not agree with me that the best advice he could give the premier of Ontario is to call an election and put the people of our province out of their misery by allowing them to get rid of the government that is keeping them in the misery that the Tories helped create?

Direct way.

That's dangerous, Iain.

The second point I want to make-
Spending like Bobbie Rae.

It used public tax dollars to protect existing jobs and slow down the outflow of jobs. It also used public money to invest in new projects, the anti-recession program. Six hundred jobs.

No. I do not know the number but at the very least 600 jobs were created in Thunder Bay.
The member is wrong. The member should stop listening to the stuff that is coming out of Queen's Park from his provincial colleagues and start looking at the figures. He should look beyond the rhetoric to find out the kind of good work the Ontario government has done.
Quite frankly if there had not been an NDP government in Ontario we would not have had the assistance to Algoma Steel in Sault Ste. Marie. We would not have had the package for Kapuskasing and we certainly would not have had the help that we got in Sapawe and Atikokan.
