speakeroldname: Mr. Michel Champagne (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and Minister of Forestry):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Forestry
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to speak this afternoon to an opposition motion to the effect that the federal government, my government, has done very little for the economy and that it sat idly by, to use the words of my colleague from the New Democratic Party, without any attempt at strengthening the economy.
I think this is a totally gratuitous, ludicrous and unfounded statement. All in all I would say it could be described as a typical NDP statement. Let me explain. History shows, and we have the figures to prove it, that when we came to power in 1984, we inherited an extremely high deficit. At that time the Prime Minister of Canada stated that one of his government's priorities would be to bring down that deficit, to help small businesses get back on their feet, and to get rid of any overlapping that existed, which would make it possible for Canadians to thrive in their country and abroad.
What did we do? First we tackled the deficit which was out of control; the government had been spending more than it was taking in and the debt was increasing dramatically. During the last few years we went from an operating deficit to an operating surplus. Except for the debt, one could say that our government, under the responsible leadership of our Prime Minister, has
April 22, 1993

succeeded in radically containing the operating deficits and replacing them with operating surpluses. Unfortunately, my opposition colleagues, the Liberals in particular, are reluctant to admit that our government's policies have produced very positive results.
Since 1984 both the Liberal and the NDP opposition have questioned the various programs and bills, even the various budgets tabled by our both past and present Ministers of Finance. Each time they called it a catastrophe. Each time a new budget was tabled in the House, they said it was worthless because Toiy budgets mean economic chaos for Canadians. Businesses will go bankrupt or will be shut down and jobs will be lost.
But when we look at what has happened since 1984 and we study figures carefully, we realize that we have helped the business sector more than before. How can we do that? Of course, the government is not going to set up businesses. I see my Liberal colleague nodding in disagreement but if he looked closely at what has happened and considered where investments were, he would see the tax breaks and the interest rate cutbacks companies have benefited from. In 1984 for a businessman who wanted to start a company, the commercial rate under a Liberal government was 12 per cent. Now, in spite of the criticism from the Liberal opposition, the commercial rate is 5.35 per cent. You can play politics. You can say whatever you want. One thing is for sure, if you have the choice of paying a 12 per cent interest rate on a million dollar loan or 5.35 per cent, any Canadian in his right mind, maybe with the exception of a Liberal, will choose to pay 5.35 per cent. That is how the federal government, the Prime Minister and our Ministers of Finance, have wanted to operate since 1984.
On one hand they tell us: You're helping companies at the expense of workers. But without companies, there are no workers. It is an equation which is fairly simple and so logical that it should not even be questioned.
On the other hand we were told: Now we have the companies but no workers who are experienced. So we should give them some training because whether we like it or not, we are open to global competition and to foreign markets. Canada is an exporting country and it needs some foreign market. The opposition told us no,
Supply
that we must stay home. They were against the free trade agreement with the United States. Now they are fighting against the agreement with Unites States and Mexico. They forget to mention one thing to Canadians and again it is very important and has no political colour: Our trade surplus with the United States was $17.5 billion last year which means hundreds and thousands of jobs in our country.
This means that jobs were saved, jobs that brought tax revenue to the government and gave our small business people in each of our municipalities and our respective ridings a living because people were able to buy and to pay. Our workers' income had an added value that was extremely important because the inflation rate last year was 1.5 per cent compared to the average of 8.8 per cent under the last Liberal government.
Figures do not lie; the figures show that the Conservative government of Prime Minister Mulroney with its finance ministers and various ministers with economic portfolios has taken concrete action to give Canadians better opportunities in the world economy.
The Conservative government is not the one saying that Canada will have the highest growth rate next year; it is the OECD, all industrialized countries that say Canada is doing well and working to overcome its financial problems created by a previous government.
We see what that does, the massive intervention of a government trying to create a parallel economy, a fictitious economy. Remember, and who does not remember-I see my colleague from Mississauga South and I am sure that in his riding he had problems in 1984 and before-when ordinary people wanted to borrow to buy a house. Interest rates were around 20 per cent; today you can get a mortgage at 9 or 10 per cent or so. This means taxpayers save 10 per cent in interest. The 10 per cent saved on a mortgage loan can be used for consumer goods. Consumer goods mean production, which means job creation, business and available capital.
I do not think that Canadians are not intelligent. On the contrary, they have been able to set themselves up in business in recent years not only in their respective provinces but also internationally. Looking at companies

April 22, 1993
Supply
like SNC Lavalin and Bombardier, which are leaders in our economy, we can say one thing: We need foreign trade in order to survive.
Not just foreign trade comes into it because as we go down to more concrete levels in our local economy we realize that our government has done a lot since 1984. Of course we have not solved everything but we have done an awful lot to revive the economy. For example, take the number of unemployed workers in 1984. When something did not work the Liberal government created a Crown corporation and all sorts of programs but in fact these were not necessarily long-term paying jobs.
I am looking at the statistics here, because we are often criticized for losing hundreds of thousands of jobs while the Conservative government did nothing. For example, in April 1992, 12,173,000 people were employed and in 1993 there were 12,376,000, an increase of
203,000	in a year. That is not so bad for a government which they say is doing nothing for the economy.
Nearly 163,000 full-time jobs were created in a year. In every Question Period, we hear the opposition say: "It is disastrous. Companies have closed down and jobs have been lost because of free trade with the Americans or free trade with Mexico." It is getting very hard to answer the opposition because when we talk to them individually, most of the sensible members in the Liberal Party tell us that, yes, a free trade agreement with the United States is essential and vital. Every one of them tells us that markets are going global and that we cannot live in isolation. Of course for partisan political reasons they can say that they want to renegotiate the agreement, reopen it and impose Canada's position.
They do not know what renegotiation means. Furthermore, I would point out to everyone listening to us that under the last Liberal government, relations with the Americans were extremely strained. We lost hundreds, even thousands of jobs because of that.
One of the daily tasks of our Prime Minister was to rebuild the confidence of the Americans in our country, to reopen markets which had been lost by the Liberal government, to try to allow Canadian businesses to
export and create jobs for Canadians. That is what we did and we can see the results today.
When we do business with our main partner, the United States, we no longer need to refer disagreements to the GATT where decisions can take three, four or even five years. We have a settlement mechanism within the free trade agreement and this has proven to be most helpful for Canadians. Look at our pork producers, for instance, and we are now working on the softwood lumber case.
I heard NDP members say that we did not do anything for the forest industry, for the pulp and paper industry. They know very well that we are going through a market restructuring and that Canada is no longer alone on international markets. Competition is fierce.
That is why, accompanied the Minister of Forestry, who is now in Europe defending the sound management of our forests accompanied by the Minister for International Trade and with the Minister of Employment and Immigration, who more than tripled and even quadrupled the budget for labour training, we are giving ourselves development tools that are very interesting.
As evidence of what I am saying, only two weeks ago the Minister of Employment and Immigration was in my riding. He announced financial assistance of $300,000 to a co-operative of forest workers who bought a business, a sawmill, at a cost of $1,500,000. They will maintain 70 jobs and open new markets.
Do you know what is interesting, Madam Speaker? A part of their new market is directed toward American markets and will reach European markets. Contrary to some prophets of doom on the Liberal side, but particularly on the NDP side, they are not scared of markets, of competition. They mostly trust their ability as workers to have in their community a profitable industry with quality products.
These are ordinary people who did that and they did it with pleasure. They did it because it was an economic challenge to keep their region strong, to allow some people to get back into business and to allow others to start new businesses.
Very shortly yet another announcement will be made in my constituency concerning an investment of $400,000 going to a sawmill, for a total of $2,800,000. A dry kiln will be built. Why a dry kiln? Because we are exporting a
April 22, 1993

lot of lumber. This particular sawmill exports a lot of its lumber, not to the Canadian market, but to foreign markets, to the United States and Europe. We have high quality phytosanitary measures and our businesses are adapting to new market conditions.
Unlike the opposition parties, the companies do not rest on their laurels and say: "Boy, everything is wrong. It is even worse than before. Nothing has changed". Quite the opposite. They seek new business opportunities because they know that in order to succeed they need to be productive and to compete not only with other Canadian or Quebec businesses but also with every international company in their industry. That is the key to success and what we have been successfully promoting since 1984.
I see my colleague from Richmond-Wolfe is here. Even if it is wrong we often say our friends from the Bloc Quebecois, our friends from the Liberal Party, our friends from the NDP. I call them friends because they are members of Parliament, but besides being parliamentarians we have nothing in common.
The hon. member for Richmond-Wolfe told me he worked hard to help, for example Domtar in Windsor which got a $40 million investment; in Disraeli $200,000 was given to a company; the RCM received $1 million through the disadvantaged areas assistance program. The same thing was done in our part of the country. The federal government negotiated Canada-Quebec and Canada-Ontario agreements. In the end, federal-provincial agreements were reached in every major economic sector.
.(1755)
We have done a lot, and we did it not just by excessively increasing government expenditures. We did it within our ability to pay, within our ability to do things without borrowing from our children's future and the future of all Canadians. Above all, we did it jointly with all the provinces and with each and every one of our partners.
I do not understand why the NDP refused to support the free trade agreement which was extremely important for Quebec and the other provinces which export to the United States. Neither do I understand why the NDP and the Liberals refused to support drug bills which were extremely important in terms of research and develop-
Supply
ment, in terms of highly skilled jobs and in terms of specialized jobs.
Similarly, I cannot see why our colleagues from the NDP and the Liberal Party voted against the unemployment insurance reform bill which allowed the Minister of Employment and Immigration to take sums of money and use them for training instead of simply encouraging workers to look for a job.
These last few years, they have refused to co-operate to stimulate the Canadian economy. They have refused to do so because in their view, it does not matter if you spend too much, it does not matter if you spend more than your operating budget since it is only somebody else's money anyway.
Today for example, when we look at our public finances, we are happy and proud to be able to say that revenues are now higher than expenditures. That is what a responsible government is all about. That is why the Richmond-Wolfe, Champlain and Mississauga ridings, and even ridings of members of the opposition, can obtain real economic action which benefit the workers and the businesses and bring in revenues.
I almost forgot; now that I see him, I remember my colleague, the member for Pontiac-Gatineau-Labelle whose efforts were focused on forestry. He worked extremely hard to push forward at least three forestry projects with federal investments in sawmills totaling over $4 million. That amount of $4 million will generate $16 million in investments will create 350 direct jobs in Pontiac-Gatineau-Labelle and who knows how many indirect jobs. We did that although the opposition, Liberals and New Democrats alike, would want the Canadian people to believe that we did nothing. Those are real achievements rather than just empty rhetoric as they often indulge in.
The opposition claims that the members on this side are silent; they are not silent. They are working to solve issues and economic problems in their respective constituencies. We can enumerate every one of them as well as the businesses which have been helped. We can even name the workers who have been helped and the programs which were implemented. Finally, we can say that in spite of the unpopular policies implemented by our government since 1984 there is hope in the eyes of Canadians. They know that we are a responsible government which makes difficult decisions and that we will be re-elected.

April 22, 1993
Private Members' Business
If I were a Liberal I would be getting concerned because the polls show that it is indeed the case. If I were a New Democrat I would not worry however, because their popularity is high before an election, but they always fall back where they belong come election time. I would worry if I belonged to the Bloc Quebecois, because they are the ones who will most likely disappear.
In the last nine years the government formed by the Progressive Conservative Party was able to give a new life to the Canadian economy. It was able to do so not only by putting money into our businesses, but by cleaning up our institutions and by managing in such a way that would make any Canadian venture a profitable one. Indeed, it is hard not to follow the example of the federal government because our revenues are higher than our expenditures and it is the net profit which benefits Canadians as a whole.
This is why I am proud to belong to a party which believes that the economy is not built by "program creators" as the Liberals did, but through joint action and harmonization by the economic sector, the workers and the governments. This is what puts our country among the ones which will experience the highest growth rate in the coming year.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George -Bulkley Valley) moved:
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should hold full public hearings before a final decision is made on the status of VIA Rail's remote routes.
He said: I am pleased to rise in debate today on an important issue to the people of Prince George-Bulk-ley Valley and northern British Columbia. The issue is the future of VIA Rail's Skeena service that runs from Prince Rupert to Prince George and through the Robson Valley on to Jasper.
The focus of the debate is my private member's motion that calls for the government to hold public hearings before deciding on the future of VIA's remote services which includes the Skeena. Before giving some background to the motion I want to say-I think I have checked the record-that this is the first time that Parliament has debated VIA's remote services to this extent, I want to thank the members who are here tonight to participate in this debate for that involvement.
Members will remember the announcement by the government in October 1989 to cut VIA services across the country by 50 per cent. Many services were eliminated completely and others were cut back. Perhaps the most notorious cut by the government was the decision to drop the fabled train called the Canadian that provided service on the Canadian Pacific route, often referred to as the southern route. This was a classic train noted all over the world and this government cancelled it. One will remember that we were to get a private service in its place. That is something yet to happen.
The government then allowed VIA to continue its northern route that was cut back to three times a week in either direction. Work has been done to improve this service and I will comment on that a little later on.
At the same time as these changes were made the government announced that eight so-called remote services operated by VIA would be reviewed by the government. I quote from the minister's release of the day: "The government will be reviewing the transportation needs of the truly isolated communities along these remote routes to determine whether more cost-effective means of access could be introduced". The future of these services was left in the hands of the Minister of Transport.
The remote services were The Pas to Lynn Lake, Wabowden to Churchill, Winnipeg to Churchill, Sudbury to White River, Senneterre to Cochrane, Montreal to
April 22, 1993

Senneterre, Montreal to Jonquiere and, of course, the Skeena.
I would like to focus my comments on the Skeena and then make some reference to general comments on the remote service. The Skeena operates between Prince Rupert, Prince George and Jasper three times a week. In the past, some time ago, it was daily and at one time served Edmonton. Conventional equipment is used and it passes some of the best scenery available for rail passengers in Canada, or in the world for that matter. The trip has been written up by foreign writers as one of VIA's best kept secrets. It even hosted CBC's Midday program at one time.
I have travelled on the train quite often and am always impressed by the trip, the terrific staff and the opportunity to see my riding and the rest of northern B.C. from a different perspective. The staff on the train have always been very helpful and are always willing to pass on their views about the need to keep the service and how to improve it. They are very dedicated to good passenger rail service.
Statistics released at the time of the cuts to VIA pointed to an expensive run but also one that, when running on a half decent schedule, generated enough traffic to be in the top third of all VIA trains and also the top of all of the remote services.
However the cuts to VIA affected the service's awareness to people. The current schedule of 3 a.m. departures from Prince George-some would question whether Prince George is on a remote service-did not make it popular with travellers. Connections in Jasper to the Transcontinental service are non-existent and are not an encouragement to travel to points east or to return from the east by train. The three days a week service is not frequent enough to give travellers the automatic knowledge of when the train will be coming or going.
All that combined with a telephone service that is not always easy to use has led to a decrease in traffic although there are still times when the train is very busy.
Following the government's decision to study the remote services I continued to impress upon the government the need to make a positive decision on VIA Rail. I kept the pressure on three different transport ministers
Private Members' Business
to make a final decision that recognized the need to keep the Skeena running. At times the government was confused about the direction to take. Letters often contradicted public statements and the decision-making process seemed to drag on, perhaps deliberately.
For example while the decision to review the service was made in October 1989, as of July 1992 the minister was still saying that a decision had not yet been made. In fact a letter which I have just recently received from the minister says that cabinet still has not had time to actually review the file, but more on that in a moment.
In order to consult with local residents along the line I along with the member for Skeena hosted a public meeting in Smithers, B.C. on September 30. We heard comments from tourist operators, local governments, chambers of commerce and people who work on the railroad itself. They all spoke about the need to keep the service, to improve the schedule and to develop a comprehensive marketing campaign. A clear consensus emerged that we had to keep the pressure on the government to make a positive decision.
Also, with the hon. member for Skeena I want to extend our thanks to our party's transport critic, the hon. member from Thunder Bay-Atikokan. He has been outspoken on the questions of VIA Rail and the disaster we now have in the country and with all the troubles in the airline industry.
Last July there was some success when the Minister of Transport visited Prince George. I issued a challenge to him to keep the service going. The minister responded by saying as reported in the Prince George Citizen on July 25, 1992: "As far as the Skeena is concerned it is still a decision of CN Rail and the Government of Canada to keep the Skeena running". He went on to say: "I am committed to see it continued".
I praised the minister and the government for this decision and was hopeful that it would be finalized and plans for the service could be developed to improve its viability and attractiveness to the travelling public. Since then we have had some good news and maybe some not so good news.
Correspondence as recent as a letter dated February 11, 1993 from the Minister of Transport would seem to indicate there is still some confusion on the part of the government as to the future of these remote services. I quote from the letter: "Although the review process for

April 22, 1993
Private Members' Business
the VTA Rail remote services is complete, cabinet has not yet had an opportunity to consider the remote services file. As I mentioned in my previous correspondence"-I might add many previous letters-"I am confident that a decision will be made as soon as possible. Thank you again for writing".
First of all I think it would be opportune and helpful to the members of this House, certainly those members who represent constituencies where there are remote services, if the minister would release that report and make it available to us. I think that would go some distance in aiding all of us who are obviously communicating with our constituents, local governments and chambers of commerce on the importance of these services.
Let us settle the confusion first. In the February 11 letter the minister continues to go on about how this file is still being studied. Three transport ministers have been doing that since October 1989.
I want to make it very clear the Minister of Transport made a public commitment to the people of northern B.C. that the Skeena was to be continued and I hold this government to that promise. The minister cannot say one thing in Prince George and another here in Ottawa. The Skeena is here to stay.
More recently VIA Rail has announced consultations regarding changes to the Skeena. This is a bit of the good news. What is being proposed for the Skeena is a daylight service with trains running from Prince Rupert to Prince George three times a week during the day and a similar service from Prince George to Jasper also during the day.
The focus will be on the tourist potential of the train and it is very clear that Prince George, the city, and its hospitality industry will be the biggest benefactors of this change. All of the communities from the Robson Valley, McBride, to Burns Lake and Houston will also benefit from the increased travel.
The travel will be at more reasonable times. It will now be possible for people from McBride as I mentioned to go to Prince George during normal hours. It will also be
possible to head west from Prince George to Bums Lake or Houston at a more reasonable departure time.
Assuming no major problems with this proposal, VIA intends to upgrade meal service on the train, add a coach, and have at least one day of good connections in Jasper to the Canadian where there are currently no convenient connections.
I should note as well that for residents of the Prince George area of northern B.C. the quickest way to travel for example to Vancouver is actually on the British Columbia Railway. This new schedule should make connections much easier with the BCR for those passengers wanting to travel by train to Vancouver.
Perhaps the most important part of the consultations from VIA Rail are VIA's plans to launch a major marketing of the service in Japan, Australia, the United States and the United Kingdom. This may be the first real promotion of the run in some time. We need the kind of promotion of the Skeena like VIA currently does of its service in central Canada.
If we had the full colour ads and the television advertising that most of us see in Ottawa and in central Canada for which VIA is perfectly in its right to do and I encourage VIA to do that, but we ask for a little fairness. If we had even a portion of that advertising and promotion revenue for Skeena clearly more people would be aware of the service. It always grates me to see the extensive advertising conducted here when there is nothing to promote the Skeena.
Even VIA's ads to promote special rates on the Canadian in western Canada do not include tickets on the Skeena. The changes VIA Rail is proposing would take effect with the April 1994 schedule. VTA says it needs time to prepare the service and to market the trip overseas.
I have already had calls to my office. Of course many people, encouraged by these hopeful changes thought they were going to happen immediately. After explaining to them that VIA feels it needs the time to change the schedule, people were comforted by that and were pleased to hear that maybe for the first time in a long time something is actually going to be done to improve and work on the service on the Skeena.
I was pleased that the president of VIA Rail, Mr. Lawless, took the time to greet the member for Skeena
April 22, 1993

and me on the change and to hear our suggestions and comments about the direction to take. It is a step in the right direction and I hope ensures the Skeena's continued operation.
There is one caution though. It was expressed to me by some residents in the community as to whether the service's new orientation would be able to attract the necessary traffic in the winter months. In other words, in improving the service to serve the expected heavier tourist use which we support, we must not forget about the regular users of the route and the system. One proposal was made to me that if there were heavier tourist potential and use in the summer it might revert to a slightly different or tailored service in the winter months..
It is my view that even more can be done. This government has to definitively state that remote services are not going to be cut. As I said earlier, the Minister of Transport has made a commitment to northern British Columbia and Prince George, but when one looks at the writing, he is less supportive here in Ottawa and he cannot have it both ways.
It is my view as well that the government must introduce a VIA Rail act so that the corporation can continue to operate on a more independent basis and not always rely on the blessing of the government of the day.
With regard to the Skeena, I also see a need to look at daily service as we once had and for an extension to Edmonton which VIA Rail was open to if the traffic should warrant it. We have seen what the improved service on the Canadian has done for the traffic on that run.
The upgrading and improvement of that particular service has attracted the ridership. People who are taking that train have been prepared to pay the price for it as well, which tells me and I hope will tell this House that when an effort is put into upgrading and improving the service people will take the train. The schedule must be convenient and there must be a marketing plan to back it up.
My motion calls on the government to hold public hearings before a decision on the remote services is made. There have been some consultations in northern B.C. with VIA Rail, the tourist operators and others
Private Members' Business
about the proposed changes to the Skeena. Those kinds of hearings have to be more extensive, in particular to the other runs in this country where the discussions are ongoing.
The first step would be for the minister to release that report. His report to cabinet should be made public so that we have the benefit of the research and knowledge of his department and the time it has put into it. Then we could circulate the report and discuss it with the communities, the chambers of commerce, the local governments, the people working on the railroad itself. We could see the direction in which the government wants to proceed and the public could have an opportunity to have their say.
The public did not have their say when the Draconian cuts were made to Via Rail in October 1989.1 think that is only fair particularly to those communities where in some cases the train is the only transportation service available. At the very least, the people in those communities should be given the opportunity to have their say.
I have fought long and hard to keep the Skeena operating and to improve its service. There is still more that can be done but to date, we have a commitment to keep it going. I am going to keep up the good fight for the people of my riding to see that this service continues.

Madam Speaker, I appreciate the hon. member's arguments in favour of public hearings.
However, I am afraid I must disagree and I intend to provide a number of statistics to show that hearings would not contribute any information that is not already available.
I wish to respond today to the hon. member's motion requesting that public hearings be held before a final decision is made on the status of VIA's remote routs. As you will recall, these services were not affected by the government's decision in 1989 to restructure the VIA Rail network.
Rather, the remote services were to become the subject of a study to determine if more cost effective options existed for providing service to truly isolated communities.
Before addressing my hon. colleague's motion, I think it might be useful if I were to elaborate somewhat on the

April 22, 1993
Private Members' Business
characteristics of the remote services, so that people will know just what it is we are talking about today.
As part of its network, VIA operates eight remote services. These eight routes operate over 3,100 miles of CN and CP railway lines in the provinces of Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba, Alberta and British Columbia.
The eight remote routes operate between the following points, which may interest our listeners: Montreal-Jonquiere;	Montreal-Senneterre;
Senneterre-Cochrane; Sudbury-White River; Winni-peg-Churchill; The Pas-Lynn Lake; and Jasper-Prince Rupert.
Generally speaking, VIA operates three return trips a week over each route. The only exceptions are along the Senneterre-Cochrane route where VIA operates only one round trip per week between Taschereau, Quebec and Cochrane, Ontario, and the Wabowden-Churchill route which sees one round trip per week.
The Wabowden-Churchill service, however, follows the same route as the Winnipeg-Churchill train, which runs three return trips a week.
The Wabowden-Churchill and The Pas-Lynn Lake services operate as mixed trains. A mixed train consists of a freight train which operates on a fixed schedule to which one or more passenger cars are attached. All the other remote services operate only as passenger trains. Coach and checked baggage service are provided on all the trains.
Sleeper and meal facilities are provided on the Montreal-Senneterre, Winnipeg-Churchill and Jasper-Prince Rupert trains which operate on overnight schedules.
Studies have shown that of the 394 points located in the remote areas served by the trains-and here are some statistics that are real eye-openers-only 45 have year-round populations with a total of 7,844 residents. Many of these 45 points are the homes of native people. So you get the picture. Of 394 points, only 45 have year-round populations, and most of those 45 points are the homes of native people.
The most recent statistics available indicate that the number of residents living at remote points on a year-round basis was 2,457 on the Montreal-Senneterre
route, 10 on the Senneterre-Cochrane route, 326 on the Sudbury-White River route, 3,002 on the Winnipeg-Churchill and Wabowden routes, 1,793 on The Pas-Lynn Lake route and 141 along the Jasper-Prince Rupert route. There are no individuals living on a year-round basis at any of the remote points identified as stops along the Montreal-Jonquiere route.
People may wonder, then, what these routes are used for. These trains are used for a variety of purposes. Certainly they provide those people who do live year-round at remote points-and there are very few, as I said earlier-with access to regional service centres for medical, shopping, educational and business opportunities.
Many of the remaining points are used on a seasonal basis. They are used for recreational purposes to access cottages and commercial lodges and camps located at remote points. Others travel into the area for hunting, boating or other recreational wilderness pursuits. Such remote service contributes to the economic activity in the area by promoting access to camps, lodges and tour operators located in remote wilderness areas.
Some individuals travel to remote points to earn their livelihoods in such areas of activity as trapping, fishing, prospecting and forestry.
That is why the trains provide a limited freight service. And that is why the statistics on service frequency, routes and population density are so important. The trains provide a limited-that is the operative word-freight service, carrying foodstuffs, essential supplies and mail to remote communities.
In 1992 approximately 42 per cent of the passengers using the remote services were destined to points which are solely served by VIA. The remaining passengers were travelling to points which are accessible by year-round highways and in some cases are also accessible by bus or air transport.
The number of travellers going to or from remote points varies considerably by service. In 1992, the percentage of passengers travelling to or from a remote point varied from 80 per cent for The Pas-Lynn Lake to 7 per cent for Jasper-Prince Rupert. In the case of the Montreal-Jonquiere service which has no permanent year-round population at any remote point, these travel-
April 22, 1993

lers are going to seasonal camps and cottages located at remote points.
In 1992 almost 108,000 passengers travelled on these services yielding an average of 42 passengers per trip operated. The level of demand, however, varied greatly. The Winnipeg to Churchill route, which at almost 1,100 miles is the longest remote service, carried an average of 101 passengers per trip. In contrast, the Senneterre-Cochrane service carried only eight passengers per trip.
Between 1988 and 1992 the ridership on these services declined by 28 per cent. These declines can be attributed to the construction of roads into the remote areas, declining populations at remote points, closure of lumber camps, and regrettably the downturn in the tourism sector which has been felt in many regions over the past several years. As well, many passengers who used the remote services to travel to points which do have other means of access appear to have shifted to alternate means such as car, bus or air to make their trips.
No one can deny that the remote services represent a complex situation. They are strung out across the northern regions of our vast country, in areas with a small and declining population. However, the cost of providing this service is accelerating. In 1992, the subsidy per passenger amounted to $250. In other words we are subsidizing a very small percentage of the travelling public. You must realize that common sense dictates we review the entire situation.
I agree that the government must look at the provision of services to remote communities in all these regions, but we must reduce costs. As a government, we are responsible for managing the resources and finances of this country. That is why I do not think it would be useful to conduct public hearings. The government must therefore take the lead and make decisions on the basis of the situation and the figures before us today and I must say we have enough information to do so.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be given the opportunity to address this private member's bill which I believe can be supported. Let me explain why.
Private Members' Business
To have full public hearings before a final decision regarding VIA Rail's remote routes is taken seems to me to be rather wise.

We could have public hearings which would last a long time, cost a lot of money, and so on, but we could also have shorter public hearings to try and confirm some statistics as my colleague was saying a moment ago. It all depends on the scope of the hearings. As far as I am concerned, I would prefer public hearings, to be absolutely sure. My friend said that situations vaiy a great deal. There are remote communities where the only access is by rail while others, although small and isolated, are better linked with the rest of the world. As far as I am concerned I would say that we should consult without taking months to do so and spending millions of dollars.
Clearly I support this motion, but I support it in a positive way since I would like public hearings to ascertain that the data we have are accurate.

As I indicated, we must make sure we see each unique situation as it is. I support a policy for the whole of Canada that looks at the smaller, isolated, very often northern communities. I think it is important that we do not simply look at one part of the nation but we do so within the whole.
I want to focus on the line to Churchill and the port of Churchill this evening. Obviously those are in my province and are particularly important to me and my province.
Some will know that I and my party colleagues sat down together and put out what we called an agenda for jobs and growth. We believe that an aggressive economic policy is the key to the creation of jobs. This is very relevant. I want my colleagues to know that I am not playing any games. We addressed a number of factors: the cultural industries, the production of ethanol which might be good for the west, a new core area agreement for the city of Winnipeg, and prairie and western integration programs because we think that we can do more things co-operatively. We looked at Winnipeg International Airport and what might be done to enhance jobs but we also looked at the port of Churchill.

I want to focus my comments on the port of Churchill. The port of Churchill has been one of the victims of the nine years of Tory economic policy. Where the Tories see this as a lost cause, and I do not say that unkindly, we see it rather as an opportunity to be seized. Obviously there is an ideological difference.
Our intent with Churchill is anchored in a very straightforward set of facts. Prairie grain producers have the opportunity to export their product through a port situated closer to their farms, closer to major export markets, which is simply less costly than the St. Lawrence seaway or the west coast. Those are facts and that is part of our statement. Churchill makes economic sense for prairie farmers and Manitoba.
I want to quote this document. This is a fact that not a lot of people know about.
For example, Churchill is approximately 1,270km from Prince Albert. But Montreal is more than 3,500km away via Thunder Bay and the Seaway. Murmansk, Russia is an important destination for Canadian grain exports. It is more than 800km closer to Churchill than to Montreal. The simple fact is that the Port of Churchill can save prairie farmers on transport costs compared to Thunder Bay and the St. Lawrence.
I continue to quote from this document.
Using Churchill is also sound environmental policy. Shorter distances mean less consumption of fossil fuels. A thriving Port and maintenance of the rail line could pave the way for economic diversification in Churchill.
fThis is extremely important.
Port facilities and a rail link make it a leading world contender as a spaceport satellite launching centre. New opportunities in Northern tourism also depend heavily on the continuation of the rail link.
It is not only for the grain. There are other possibilities, for example tourism. Again to quote from this particular report:
Yet the rail link and all its spin-off benefits depend on grain exports through the Port of Churchill. The Port requires 600,000 tonnes per year to break even.
This is a fact.
However, in the last several years it has seen less than 300,000 tonnes.
Therefore, it has been losing money.
The Port could easily handle 1,000,000 tonnes per year without difficulty and without expensive upgrading of either the rail link or the Port facility itself.
We believe that.
Exciting opportunities are within reach for Churchill. For example talks are under way on barter arrangements with Russia which would see Canadian grain exports paid for with phosphate rock. Churchill could be the linchpin in substantial two-way trade flows between the prairies and the new democracies of Europe.
I complete this quote by saying that my colleagues and I want to press any new government for the export of one million tonnes of grain through the port of Churchill each year.
While I have deliberately focused my remarks on the port of Churchill, I think we have to do an in-depth analysis on the others as well. While I suspect my colleague's statistics, and they were impressive, are really quite accurate, it is particularly important to ensure that we look at each unique situation. Without exaggerating costs, because I am sensitive to those as well, particularly in today's economy, it would be foolhardy not to have public hearings so that we can make sure that whatever decisions are taken are sound for the people in those various communities.
I could not agree more. I do not want public hearings for the sake of it, but I would like to try and establish what the best solution is for each remote community concerned.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to support my colleague's motion which the House should adopt, requiring public hearings before any decision is made on the remote services of VIA Rail.
Let me begin by asking, where is the report? When the then Minister of Transport announced in succession the elimination of 50 per cent of VIA Rail services in the fall of 1989 and the Prime Minister announced the creation of the royal commission on passenger transportation at the same time, the minister also said, and my colleague read a quote from the press release, that they would do a study of the remote routes to look at alternate ways of providing services. There are a number of Canadians who can only leave their communities by rail. There is no road, there is no air service, and in some cases there is no water service, certainly not of the commercial variety. They are captive.

Private Members' Business
I know for a fact, and it is in the public record, that the Department of Transport finished the report quite some time ago. I believe it was almost eight or nine months ago when I heard it was completed and they were just waiting for time on the cabinet agenda.
While we are all happy they are continuing the remote services, there is a level of uncertainty out there. I challenge the government today. I hope the next government member that stands in his or her place to speak on this motion will tell the House why it is the Minister of Transport cannot get time at the cabinet table to talk about alternatives for the remote rail services.
Is it because cabinet members already know what is in it? Do they know that the price tag for providing alternate services, either road or air, is too expensive? Conversely do they know that the price tag for relocating those 7,844 permanent residents along those eight lines is also excessive? Or maybe whatever is in that report is as bad as the original decision was and the government does not want to add any more nails to its coffin as it goes into the federal election.
I encourage the government member to report to the House. I encourage the Minister of Transport to report to the House and tell us what is happening with that.
I mentioned uncertainty. The member for Prince George-Bulkley Valley has done an incredible amount of work keeping the issue of the Skeena alive in his area to the point where the Minister of Transport, I assume at the beck of the government member for that area, told chamber of commerce members, as reported in the Prince George Citizen on July 25, 1992:
Corbeil told Chamber members at Friday's luncheon his commitment to maintain VIA Rail's Skeena service through Prince George is firm.
"As far as the Skeena is concerned, it's still a decision of CN Rail and the Government of Canada to keep it running," he said. "My colleague, Frank Oberle, said the line would go only over his dead body.
"I wouldn't want to be responsible for him shooting himself," Corbeil added, eliciting laughter. 'And so I'm committed to see it (Skeena) continued."
Yet we hear that they are still studying it, that they do not have the report to cabinet and that cabinet has not made a decision. There is that uncertainty.
There is also uncertainty every place east of Winnipeg. Independent of what the government is doing-in fact the government has said that it will not intervene in any way-CN and CP are working together to roll up as many tracks as they can. CN has already applied to sell its line from Truro to Sydney, Nova Scotia. CP has applied to abandon its line from Sherbrooke, Quebec, to Saint John, New Brunswick, a line which contains VIA Rail services that I used not too long ago. They are combining operations in the Ottawa Valley which will have an effect on VIA Rail services. They are looking at consolidation of operations east of Winnipeg.
When the government member spoke he forgot one of the remote lines, one of the protected lines. It is the line that goes from Capreol to Winnipeg. It is the line that the Transcontinental is on. The reason the Transcontinental goes on the northern line where there are fewer people as opposed to the southern line where there are hundreds of thousands of people, a line that goes through the north shore of Lake Superior, the city of Thunder Bay, Dryden and Kenora to Winnipeg, is that the northern line is a protected line. There are communities along there that have no alternative services. VIA decided to forgo the revenue it would get on the southern line, and a lot of people used that train on the southern line, because it had to keep services on the northern line.
In my discussions with Mr. Lawless he indicated that if we were to relocate the current three times a week service that runs on the CN northern line to the CP line to the south along the north shore of Lake Superior, that in itself would not cost much more than it does today in terms of operation costs or level of subsidy. To provide a local service much like we have in some of the other remote lines would cost a subsidy of about $12 million or $13 million per year. I do not know whether that takes into consideration the increased revenue on the southern line that would offset some of that, but that is part of the reality.
CN and CP are looking at consolidating their operations from Winnipeg through Thunder Bay on to Ca-

preol and Sudbury. If the two railways decide to do as indicated in a report done for the National Transportation Review Commission and the northern CN line which is currently the home of the Transcontinental VIA service is abandoned, that passenger service will be relocated to the southern line.
What happens to those people who live along that northern line whose only way out today is by rail? I grant that there are not hundreds of thousands of them. I take the member at his word that there are roughly 7,800 to 7,900 permanent residents. There are also a lot of working class folks who have what we may call cottages in other parts of Canada but we call camps up our way. They are not elaborate. They are not insulated. There is no electricity. Basically there are walls, a roof, a floor, some windows, a door and some bunk-beds. It is the kind of recreation a lot of working people in the cities of Winnipeg, Thunder Bay and Sudbury can afford.
There is also a lot of industry along those lines, industry such as the tourism outfitters that rely on that remote service to stimulate the economy of this nation. They attract people from the United States, Europe and Asia into those camps. They need the rails to get there. It may not show up on VIA's books but it certainly shows up on our balance of payments and it certainly shows up in the taxation applied both federally and provincially to tourist outfitters and the people who work for them. The member suggests we should have public hearings before any changes are made. I would like to remind the House the last time the only public hearings were by the
transport committee after the decision was made, trying to derail it. It had no luck.
I took the matter to the Federal Court of Appeal twice and lost both times. In fact, I am still paying some of the bills. That was the only public review.
At the very least if services are going to be eliminated or replaced, there should be public hearings. There should be environmental assessments. It may be doing more damage to punch a road through the natural environment than to continue the rail services. I could go on and on.
I would encourage the House to support my colleague's motion because there is a lot of great rail service out there. I rode the E & N last week. I took it to Nanaimo and met my colleague from Nanaimo-Cowi-chan to talk about the rail issues that affect his community. It is a great service. It is like a remote service even though it is not remote. We need those kinds of services in this country.
